# qb45dec

Decompiles MS-DOS `.OBJ` files produced by **Microsoft QuickBASIC 4.5** back
into BASIC.

Needs nothing but Python 3 — no pip install, no third-party modules. The
8086 decoder, the OMF reader and the BASIC lifter are all in this repository.

```bash
python3 qb45dec.py PROGRAM.OBJ          # writes PROGRAM.bas
python3 qb45dec.py PROGRAM.OBJ -o -     # to stdout
python3 qb45dec.py verify PROGRAM.OBJ   # structural check of the object file
python3 qb45dec.py info PROGRAM.OBJ     # externals, string literals, DATA count
python3 qb45dec.py disasm PROGRAM.OBJ   # annotated disassembly
python3 qb45dec.py split PROGRAM.OBJ    # separate trailing junk from the module
python3 qb45dec.py runtime              # the runtime routine table
```

## What comes back, and what doesn't

**Recovered exactly.** BC emits a call to a runtime separator (`B$EVCK` when
the program uses event trapping, otherwise `B$LINA`) after every source
statement, which gives exact statement boundaries. With those:

- every statement, in source order
- all string literals and numeric constants, from the `BC_CN` segment
- all `DATA` statements, byte-identical — BC stores their text in `BC_DS`,
  each prefixed with the code address of the statement it came from, which is
  also how `RESTORE <label>` finds them
- `FOR`/`NEXT`, including `STEP`
- the shape of every expression, since the emulated x87 stack can be walked
  symbolically

**Lost in compilation, and approximated.**

- *Variable names.* Gone entirely. Slots are named `n1!`, `i2%`, `s3$`,
  `arr4%()` in order of first appearance, with the type inferred from how the
  code touches each slot; `--raw-names` names them by data-segment offset
  instead.
- *Line numbers.* Labels are code offsets (`L11B9:`).
- *Block structure.* `IF`/`ELSE`, `DO`/`LOOP`, `WHILE`/`WEND` and
  `SELECT CASE` all compile to conditional jumps. The structurer folds the
  shapes it can prove safe — it refuses whenever something outside a candidate
  range jumps into it — and leaves the rest as `IF ... THEN GOTO`, which is
  always correct if less pretty. `--no-structure` turns folding off entirely.
- *`SUB`/`FUNCTION`.* Procedures appear as `GOSUB` targets. A module that
  defines real procedures exports them as PUBDEF records, which are reported
  but not yet turned into `SUB` blocks.

## How it works

| stage | file | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| OMF | `qb45dec/omf.py` | parses and verifies the record stream, rebuilds a byte image per segment, resolves every relocation (including the thread-encoded ones) to a segment, group or external name, and recovers the `DATA` text |
| decode | `qb45dec/x86.py` | 16-bit x86 decoder with structured operands. BC compiles floating point to `INT 34h`–`INT 3Dh` — the Microsoft emulator interface — so those are decoded back into the x87 instructions they stand for |
| runtime | `qb45dec/runtime.py` | maps runtime entry points to BASIC statements, each tagged `known` / `likely` / `guess` |
| lift | `qb45dec/lift.py` | symbolic execution of the x87 stack and the argument pushes; produces statements |
| structure | `qb45dec/structure.py` | folds jumps back into `FOR`, `IF`/`ELSE`, `DO`/`LOOP` |
| emit | `qb45dec/emit.py` | renders the listing |

Two conventions worth recording, since neither is documented anywhere:

- **Optional arguments** are pushed as *(present-flag, value)* pairs followed
  by a mask word. `LOCATE 7, 36` is pushed as `1, 7, 1, 36, 4`; `SCREEN 9` as
  `1, 9, 2`.
- **Graphics coordinates** are passed *before* the statement call, not as
  arguments to it: `B$N1I2` sets the first point and `B$N2I2` the second, so
  `LINE` calls both and `CIRCLE`/`PSET`/`PUT` call only the first. The `R4`
  variants take single-precision coordinates, which arrive on the stack
  (`sub sp,4` / `fstp [bx]`) rather than through `push`.
- **Arrays** reach a graphics statement as a far pointer held in the constant
  pool and relocated by the linker, so the array's identity comes from a
  relocation inside `BC_CN`, not from the instruction stream.
- **String functions** return a descriptor in `AX`, which the caller pushes
  straight into the next call, so a concatenation chain has to be followed
  through the register.

## Confidence

`python3 qb45dec.py runtime` lists every routine the decompiler knows with a
confidence tag. `known` means the mapping was confirmed from compiled evidence
that can only mean one thing — a centred column, a screen mode, an audible
frequency. Anything not in the table is emitted as a comment naming the
routine and its arguments, so an unknown call is visible rather than silently
wrong.

## Tests

```bash
python3 selftest.py
```

Checks both sample objects end to end: that they parse, that the `DATA`
recovery consumes the whole string segment, that every source statement lifts
to at least one line, that every byte of the code segment decodes with no
gaps, that known-correct statements appear in the output, and that no register
name or internal placeholder ever leaks into the listing. The decoder was also differentially tested against capstone over
6,294 instructions from these two modules; the only differences are two
cosmetic naming classes (`INT 3Dh`, which is the emulator's `FWAIT`, and
`cwd`).

## Scope

QuickBASIC 4.5 single-module objects. Object libraries (`.LIB`) are detected
and reported but not decompiled. Concatenated modules in one file are handled.
Other BASIC compilers (BASCOM 6/PDS, VB-DOS) use a related runtime and would
mostly work, but the runtime table is not tuned for them.

# regexp.library

Classic Amiga programs that need real regular expressions — not just AmigaDOS `ParsePattern()` wildcards — have long relied on ports of Henry Spencer's engine from the University of Toronto. That code compiles a pattern once into an internal program, then matches it against strings with capture-group support. It underpins the grep/ex/awk style of pattern matching familiar from BSD and NetBSD.

An earlier Amiga shared library, **RegExp.library** (Stephen Moehle, 1991 — preserved in `archive/RegExpLib/`), wrapped regexp code from the public-domain **bawk** clone for C and ARexx. It exposes a **different API** (`RegExpCompile`, `RegExpMatch`, `RegExpQuery`, …) and is **not binary-compatible** with the lineage documented here. The syntax and function names are similar in spirit, but LVO numbering, structure layout, and calling conventions do not match.

**regexp.library** — ported to AmigaOS by **Matthias Bethke** in **1998** — wraps Spencer's **NetBSD `regexp.c` v1.7** (itself built on alterations by John Gilmore and James A. Woods) as a standard four-function shared library: compile, match, free, and translate error codes. The API mirrors the familiar `RegComp` / `RegExec` / `RegFree` pattern used across BSD-derived toolchains.

This **38.2** release from the **amigazen project** is a BSD-licensed refactor of Bethke's classic 68k library for **NDK 3.2** and the **ToolKit** standard: canonical **SFD** headers, CLib39x-style startup (`StartUp.c` + `LibInit.c`), modern `__ASM__` / `__REG__` / `__SAVE_DS__` LVO definitions, expanded autodocs with **WARNING** and **BUGS** sections, the **RegTest** harness covering all four public LVOs, and a C example client. The function table, `regexp` handle layout, and application-facing ABI remain those of Bethke's **38.1** line.

## [amigazen project](http://www.amigazen.com)

*A web, suddenly*

*Forty years meditation*

*Minds awaken, free*

**amigazen project** is using modern software development tools and methods to update and rerelease classic Amiga open source software. Projects include a new AWeb, a new Amiga Python 2, and the ToolKit project — a universal SDK for Amiga development. All *amigazen project* releases are guaranteed to build against the ToolKit standard so that anyone can download and begin contributing straightaway without having to tailor the toolchain for their own setup.

This **38.2** release is still Matthias Bethke's original code, built on Henry Spencer's regexp engine. The amigazen project has refactored the build system, SDK headers, startup layout, autodocs, and tests for NDK 3.2 and ToolKit without replacing the core library implementation. It is redistributed under the BSD 2-Clause License (see [LICENSE.md](LICENSE.md)).

The amigazen project philosophy is based on openness:

*Open* to anyone and everyone — *Open* source and free for all — *Open* your mind and create!

PRs for all projects are gratefully received at [GitHub](https://github.com/amigazen/). While the focus now is on classic 68k software, it is intended that all amigazen project releases can be ported to other Amiga-like systems including AROS and MorphOS where feasible.

## History

**regexp.library** in this repository traces a line from Spencer's University of Toronto sources through NetBSD to Bethke's 1998 Amiga shared library. An unrelated earlier port, **RegExp.library**, predates it on Aminet-style archives but belongs to a separate API family.

| Era | Version | Lineage | Maintainer | Notes |
|-----|---------|---------|------------|-------|
| 1986–87 | — | Original engine | Henry Spencer (U of T) | University of Toronto regexp; freeware |
| 1986–87 | — | Engine alterations | John Gilmore, James A. Woods | `\n`, `\<` `\>`, optimisations |
| 1991 | 1.0 | **RegExp.library** | Stephen Moehle | bawk-derived; `RegExpCompile` / `RegExpMatch`; ARexx; **different ABI** |
| 1998-02-20 | 37.1 | 68k **regexp.library** | Matthias Bethke | First Bethke release; NetBSD `regexp.c` v1.7 |
| 1998-02-26 | 37.2 | 68k | Matthias Bethke | `RegXlatError()`; compile/exec optimisations |
| 1998-02-26 | 38.1 | 68k | Matthias Bethke | Last public Aminet release (readme: "Version: 38") |
| 2026 | 38.2 | **amigazen release** | amigazen project | ToolKit / SFD modernisation, RegTest, autodoc warnings |

See [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) for per-release detail.

## The compile–match–free pattern

regexp.library follows the same lifecycle as the BSD/NetBSD API Bethke ported:

| Phase | What happens |
|-------|----------------|
| **RegComp** | Compile a pattern string into an opaque `regexp` handle (library allocates storage) |
| **RegExec** | Match the handle against a string; returns `1` (match), `0` (no match), or `-1` (error) |
| **RegFree** | Release handle storage when done |
| **RegXlatError** | After failure, translate the numeric `IoErr()` code to readable text |

On compile or exec failure, read **`IoErr()`** — values are the `REXPERR_*` constants in `<libraries/regexp.h>`. Capture groups (up to **`NSUBEXP`**, 10) are available via `startp[]` / `endp[]` in the handle after a successful match.

**What regexp.library is not:** an ARexx function library (see Moehle's **RegExp.library** for that era), a DOS `ParsePattern()` replacement with identical syntax, or binary-compatible with **RegExp.library**. See `SDK/Autodocs/regexp.doc` **WARNING** sections for handle ownership and error handling.

## About regexp.library

`regexp.library` exposes **four public LVOs** for Spencer-style regular expression matching:

| Function | Role |
|----------|------|
| `RegComp` | Compile a pattern (`STRPTR`) to an internal `regexp` handle |
| `RegFree` | Free storage allocated by `RegComp` |
| `RegExec` | Match handle against a string; optional capture groups |
| `RegXlatError` | Translate `IoErr()` error code to descriptive text |

Include `<proto/regexp.h>`, define `struct Library *RegexpBase`, open with `OpenLibrary("regexp.library", 38)`, and link against `regexp.library`.

### Examples and tests

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `SDK/Examples/regexample.c` | Minimal compile / match / error client |
| `Source/unittests/regtest.c` | Unit harness (ported from Bethke's E-language `regtest.e`) |

Build from `Source/` with `smake all`; run tests with `smake unittests` then `cd unittests && smake test`. Regenerate SDK headers from `SDK/SFD/regexp_lib.sfd` with **LibDescConverter**, then copy `SDK/Include_h/` to `Source/include/`.

### Lineage compatibility

| Library | Era | Relationship to this tree |
|---------|-----|----------------------------|
| **68k Bethke / amigazen** | 37.x–38.2 | **Target ABI** — this release |
| **RegExp.library** (`archive/RegExpLib/`) | 1991 | Similar purpose, **different API and LVO table** — do not mix headers or binaries |
| **NetBSD / Spencer originals** | 1980s | Algorithm source; not Amiga shared-library API |

## Contact

- At GitHub https://github.com/amigazen/regexp.library/
- On the web at http://www.amigazen.com/ (Amiga browser compatible)
- Or email toolkit@amigazen.com

## Acknowledgements

The regular expression engine was originally written by **Henry Spencer** (University of Toronto, 1986) and altered by **John Gilmore** and **James A. Woods**. **Matthias Bethke** ported NetBSD `regexp.c` v1.7 to AmigaOS as **regexp.library** (1998). An earlier Amiga port, **RegExp.library**, is by **Stephen Moehle** (1991). This **38.2** ToolKit release is by the **amigazen project** (2026).

## License

Spencer granted permission to use and redistribute the code freely, subject to: (1) no warranty or liability on the author; (2) the origin must not be misrepresented; (3) altered versions must be plainly marked and not passed off as the original. That header is the **canonical licence** for the engine; Gilmore, Woods, and Bethke alterations are marked there as required. Do not replace or supersede it.

**Amiga port and ToolKit layers.** Matthias Bethke's Amiga shared-library wrapper (1998) and the amigazen project build, SDK, startup, and test additions (2026) are under the **BSD 2-Clause License** in [LICENSE.md](LICENSE.md). Those terms apply to Bethke/amigazen files and to redistribution of the combined work **in addition to** complying with Spencer's conditions for the engine portion.

# OH MUMMY AGAIN

**Oh Mummy Again** is a remake of **Oh Mummy** Amstrad version. It has been developed in java and libGDX.

## HISTORY AND INSTRUCTIONS

*You have been appointed head of an archeological expedition, sponsored by the British Museum, and have been sent to Egypt to explore newly found pyramids. Your party, initialy, consists of five members. Your task is to enter the five levels of each pyramid, and recover from them five Royal Mummies and as much treasure as you can.*

*Each level has already been partly uncovered by local workers and it is up to your team to finish the dig. Unfortunately, the workers digging aroused Guardians left behind by the ancient Egyptian Pharoahs to protect their royal tombs. Each level has 2 Guardian Mummies, one lies hidden while the other goes in search of the intruders.*

*The partly excavated levels are in the from of a grid made up of twenty 'boxes'. To uncover a 'box', move your team along the four sides of the box from each corner to the next. Not all boxes need to be uncovered to enable you to go through the Exit and into the next level.*

*Each level contains, ten Treasure boxes, six empty boxes, and the rest hold a Royal Mummy, a Guardian Mummy, a Key and a Scroll. If you uncover the box holding the Guardian Mummy, it will dig it's way out and persue you. Being caught by a Guardian Mummy kills one member of your team and the Mummy, unless that is, you have uncovered the Scroll. The Magic Scroll will allow you to be caught by a Guardian, without any harm to your team. The Scroll works only on the level on which found, it will only destroy one Guardian.*

*There are two ways to gain points, one is by uncovering the Royal Mummy, the other, by uncovering Treasure. When the boxes holding the Key and the Royal Mummy have been uncovered, you will be able to leave the level. Any remaining Guardians will be able to follow you onto the next level. After completing all 5 levels of a pyramid you will, when you leave the fifth level, move to level 1 of the next pyramid. When you have completed a pyramid, your success will be rewarded either by bonus points or the arrival of an extra member for your team.*

*The Guardians in the next pyramid, having been warned by those you have escaped from, will be more alert, so you from one pyramid to the next, it will pay to be even more careful.*

## CONTROLS

You can control your team by using either a Joystick (only Xbox 360 controller compatible models work) or the keyboard.

The keyboard keys are:

- **UP**: *Q* or *Up arrow*
- **DOWN**: *A* or *Down arrow*
- **LEFT**: *O* or *Left arrow*
- **RIGHT**: *P* or *Right arrow*
- **PAUSE**: *ESCAPE*

## HOW TO EXECUTE OH MUMMY AGAIN

This project is managed by Gradle. You need to have installed Java JDK 11 version or newly, and Gradle (the most recent version).

Then, you can execute

        $ gradle desktop:run

from the root directory.

## DOWNLOAD BINARIES

You can download the native Linux and Windows binaries [here](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1pcLsaNu4rQGRMm0K044AHlXxlFtOLwnv?usp=sharing).

# Another World Swiss Army Knife (awsak)

Another World Swiss Army Knife is a command-line tool for extracting and manipulating resources from 
Another World game for MSDOS.

At its current state, it's a very minimalistic and incomplete implementation, and was only
used for [Another World Hebrew](https://github.com/gmegidish/another-world-hebrew) project.

For technical details about how this cli tool came to be, as well as other projects I've made during 
the years regarding Another World and [Heart of The Alien](https://hota.sf.net), you are welcome to read 
at the [Another World Hebrew](https://github.com/gmegidish/another-world-hebrew) page. 

## Features

- Extract (unpack) resources from memlist
- Pack resources back into memlist
- Decompile bytecode into assembly code
- Compile assembly code into bytecode
- Convert background resource to a bmp
- Convert shapes into .svg files

## Installation

To get started, simply npm install *awsak* globally:

```bash
npm install -g git+https://github.com/gmegidish/awsak.git
```

or just git clone this repository manually with
```bash
git clone https://github.com/gmegidish/awsak.git
```

## Usage

```bash
awsak --help
```

```text
Usage: Another World Swiss Army Knife - awsak [options] [command]

Options:
  -V, --version        output the version number
  -h, --help           display help for command

Commands:
  extract [options]    Extract files
  pack [options]       Pack files
  compile [options]    Compile assembly to bytecode
  decompile [options]  Decompile bytecode into assembly
  pic2bmp [options]    Convert a .pic resource into .bmp
  help [command]       display help for command
```

## Extracting and Packing Resources

Awsak can extract and pack resources back to what is called a memlist. The MSDOS distribution of Another World included these files:

```text
ANOTHER.EXE
MEMLIST.BIN
BANK01
BANK02
BANK03
BANK04
BANK05
BANK06
BANK07
BANK08
BANK09
BANK0A
BANK0B
BANK0C
BANK0D
```

To extract resources, use the `extract` command. Where `disk` is the source directory that includes the files listed above.

```bash
awsak extract --indir disk --outdir resources
```

Upon completion, our `resources` directory will contain these files (and many others):

```text
0010.snd
0011.bin
0012.pic
0013.pic
0014.pal
0015.txt
0016.shp
```

While there are no filenames in the `memlist.bin` file, awsak will use the resource number as the filename, 
and the resource type as extension:

```text
snd - sound files
pic - 320x200 images (used for logos and some complicated backgrounds)
pal - palette files (32 palettes of 16 colors)
txt - script files
shp - shapes files (vector graphics)
```

To back the resources back into a memlist file, use the `pack` command. So to reverse the process, simply run:

```bash
awsak pack --indir resources --outdir disk
```

One thing you will notice, is that current implementation does not support lzss compression when packing. This means that the output files are larger than the originals on disk.

## Modifying Scripts

Another World was written on an Amiga using GFA-Basic. It features a bytecode implementation (a virtual machine) that allowed it to be ported easily to every platform imagined. This virtual machine supports 64 threads running in cooperative mode, with maximum code size of 64KB, and a memory layout of 256 variables. 

Awsak can decompile this bytecode into assembly code, and then compile it back into bytecode form. It was important to keep the format of the files as close as to Eric Chahi's original implementation. You can refer to the technical explanation of the instruction set [here](https://anotherworld.fr/another_world.htm).  

![Screenshot of Eric's editor](https://anotherworld.fr/images/another_world/editeur2.gif)

An output disassembly file will look like this:

```javascript
        seti    v1      50
L0139:  break
        dbra    v1      L0139
        seti    v1      35
        seti    v255    5
L0146:  break
        text    400     3       168     11 // Good evening professor.
        dbra    v1      L0147
        seti    v1      49
        seti    v255    5
L0159:  break
        text    401     3       168     11 // I see you have driven here in your\nFerrari.
        dbra    v1      L0159
        setvec  8       L0290
        break
```

## Development

Once you git clone the repository, and install the dependencies, you are good to go.

You can run the cli without compiling it first using: 
```bash
ts-node src/cli.ts
```

Alternatively, if you want to make sure program is ready for distribution:
```bash
npm remove -g awsak
npm run build
npm install -g .
awsak --help
```

## Future Work

- Add support for lzss compression
- Add support for custom palettes
- Add support for sound resources
- Convert svg files back to shape resources

You may submit an issue [here](https://github.com/gmegidish/another-world-hebrew/issues).

## Contribution

You might find awsak useful for your own project, but missing some functionality. If you want to help, 
please open an issue or a pull request. 

As a rule of thumb, it's always preferred to submit small a PR instead of one unmaintainable patch. I'll 
do my best to review and merge as soon as possible.

## References

* [Another World](https://www.mobygames.com/game/564/out-of-this-world/) on MobyGames
* [Another World](https://www.gog.com/en/game/another_world_20th_anniversary_edition) on GOG
* [Another World](https://anotherworld.fr/another_world.htm) on Eric Chahi's website. Includes screenshots of editor and bytecode language.
* Cyx's [Another World Interpreter](https://github.com/cyxx/rawgl) with support for most released versions.
* [Fabien Sanglard's Another World](https://fabiensanglard.net/another_world_polygons/index.html) with detailed technical explanation of the game's engine.

# Dungeon Master 64

A Commodore 64 port of FTL's *Dungeon Master* (Atari ST, 1987), written in C for cc65. It's
built from **your own copy of the original disk**: the build reads `Dungeon Master.stx` and
converts the real dungeon, texts, object names and rules tables. The C64 engine around them is
new code, not a decompile.

![A mummy on level 2, in VICE](docs/screenshot-mummy.png)
![A champion's mirror in the Hall of Champions, in VICE](docs/screenshot-mirror.png)
![A chest, bones and torch holders, in VICE](docs/screenshot-items.png)

*A mummy on level 2; Elija in his mirror in the Hall of Champions; a chest, some bones and
torch holders. Everything in the view is DM's own pictures, in a multicolour bitmap; the mummy
is DM's own picture as C64 sprites. Screenshots from VICE.*

None of the game's data is in the source files. `tools/dmconv.py` extracts it into `gen/` and
`bin/` at build time. Don't share those folders or the disk image they produce.

## What you need

- **A C64 with a RAM expansion**: an REU (512K or more) or a SuperCPU. The 14 levels, the
  overlays and the pictures the view is drawn from are kept in far memory through the
  [FarMem](../Tedide/samples/FarMem) library. Only the level the party is on sits in the C64's
  own RAM. In VICE, use `-reu -reusize 512`.
- **A 1581 disk drive** or something that acts as one (an SD2IEC, an Ultimate, VICE): the game
  is a D81 image, as a 1541's disk can't hold it and two saved games.
- To build: Python 3, cc65 (`C:\cc65`), VICE 3.x (for `c1541`), and Tedide's FarMem sources in
  `..\Tedide\samples\FarMem`.

## Building and running

```powershell
.\build.ps1          # convert, compile, make bin\dm64.d81
.\build.ps1 -Run     # ...and start it in VICE with a 512K REU
```

In VS Code, `.vscode/tasks.json` has the same as tasks: **Build** (Ctrl+Shift+B), **Run**,
**Build and run**, and **Run with mouse** (a 1351 in port 1). They assume VICE in
`C:\GTK3VICE-3.9-win64`; change the path there if yours is elsewhere.

Or open `DM64.tsln` in Tedide. It builds the FarMemC64 library, runs the converter as a
pre-build step and makes the disk image as a post-build step. Its VICE arguments attach the disk
image and add the REU.

The disk holds seven files: `DM64` (the program), and `DMHI`, `DMLEV`, `DMOVL`, `DMSPR`, `DMTXT`
and `DMWAL` (characters and the panel, levels, overlays, creature sprites, texts, and the view's
pictures). On a real machine: `LOAD"DM64",8,1` then `RUN`. `DMWAL` is packed on the disk
(about 190K) and unpacked into far memory as the game starts, so loading takes a while on a
real 1581; a fast loader, an SD2IEC or an Ultimate helps.

Saved games go on the same disk, as `DMSAVE1` and `DMSAVE2`. A save holds only the levels the
party has been on, packed: about 10 blocks early on, up to about 120 with every level visited,
so both slots always fit. Both
`build.ps1` and Tedide's post-build step (`tools\mkdisk.ps1`) keep them when they remake the
disk image. A save only loads into a build made from the same game data, and `SAVE_VERSION` in
`src/save.c` must go up whenever the saved structures change.

## Playing

You start outside the Hall of Champions. Walk in, look into the mirrors, and recruit up to four
champions. Each comes with their real statistics and possessions from the original.

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| W / cursor up | Forward |
| S / cursor down | Back |
| A, D | Step left, right |
| Q / cursor left, E / cursor right | Turn left, right |
| Space | Press what's ahead: a wall switch, keyhole, door button or mirror; take from or put into an alcove |
| T | Take an object (from the wall ahead, or from the floor) |
| G | Put down what's in your hand (into an alcove ahead, or on the floor) |
| 1-4 | That champion attacks with the weapon in their action hand |
| I | Inventory: A-O swap your hand with a slot, 1-4 pick a champion, X eat/drink/read |
| X | Eat, drink or read what's in your hand |
| C | Cast a spell (see below) |
| P | The map of the level, as far as the party has seen it |
| H | Help |
| F1, F3 | Save, load (slot 1 or 2). When the party dies, F3 loads a game |
| M | Mouse: off, a 1351 mouse in port 1, or a pointer moved by a joystick in port 2 |

The game runs in real time, as the original does. Creatures move and attack whether you press
keys or not.

### Mouse

With the pointer on, everything can be clicked:

- **The view:** the wall, door or mirror ahead presses it, as Space does. The floor (the lower
  part of the view) takes an object, or puts down what's in your hand.
- **A champion's name or bars** (under the view): opens their inventory. **Their hand** (the
  line under the bars): attacks.
- **The buttons beside the view:** **CAST**, **SAVE**, **LOAD**, **HELP** and **MAP** do what
  they say. The pad under them: turn left, forward, turn right; step left, back, step right.
- **The status line** under the party (what's in hand, what's on the floor): takes an object, or
  puts down what's in your hand.
- **The inventory:** a slot swaps it with your hand.
- **Casting:** the runes on offer, then **CAST**, **BACK** or **CANCEL**.
- **The right button** backs out of any screen.

A 1351's buttons share lines with the keyboard, so the C64 sees phantom key presses while one
is down; the game throws those away. Mouse support is new and has had little testing yet.

### Magic

Press C, choose who casts, then pick runes with 1-6, one row at a time: a power rune (LO, UM, ON,
EE, PAL, MON), then up to three more from the element, form and class rows. Each rune costs
mana as you pick it; DEL takes the last one back. RETURN casts and SPACE gives up. The game
waits while you choose, unlike the original. The spells are DM's own. The dungeon's scrolls and
walls teach some of them: VI into an empty flask heals, FUL IR is a fireball, and ZO opens doors.
A spell needs a skill level of its own level plus the power. A caster short of it may fail,
though less often the wiser they are.

## What's in it

### Taken from the original disk

- All 14 levels, square by square, with every door, pit, staircase, teleporter, fake wall,
  pressure plate, switch, keyhole, alcove, text, creature and object where FTL put them.
- The dungeon's texts (wall writing, messages, scrolls, champion descriptions), decoded from
  DM's 5-bit packed format.
- Object names, and the rules tables from `GRAPHICS.DAT`: weapon damage and weight, armour
  defence, which slots each object fits, and each creature type's speed, attack, defence,
  poison and dexterity, and which creatures are non-material. These are FTL's own LZW-packed
  tables, unpacked by `tools/dmgfx.py`.
- The spell table: all 25 spells' runes, required skill levels, skills, kinds and strengths,
  and the runes' mana costs.
- **The creatures' own pictures**: every creature's front view from `GRAPHICS.DAT`, in DM's
  palette with each creature's colour replacements, shrunk to C64 multicolour sprites by
  `tools/dmimg.py`. FTL's picture packing was decoded with the help of ScummVM's Dungeon
  Master engine.
- **The view's own pictures**: DM's floor, ceiling, walls, door frames, its four kinds of
  door with their ornaments (iron bars you can see through, locks, jewels) and buttons, its
  stairs, its 60 wall ornaments (switches, levers, locks, alcoves, torch holders, fountains,
  the champions' mirrors with their portraits), floor ornaments (pressure pads, grates, moss),
  pits, teleporter fields, the objects lying about, spells in flight, and its engraved
  lettering for writing on walls. They're cut, shrunk and placed as DM does it (the tables
  come from ScummVM's engine), including the ornaments DM scatters on plain walls at random,
  and converted to C64 multicolour by `tools/dmview.py`.

### The engine

- A first-person view the size of DM's (224x136), in a multicolour bitmap above the text, built
  as DM builds it: the floor and ceiling, then for each square far to near its walls and their
  ornaments, doors, stairs, pits, floor ornaments, objects, spells and teleporter fields. A
  raster interrupt switches from the bitmap to text partway down the screen. Messages on the
  floor appear below. The view is drawn straight onto the screen (there's no room for a second
  one), so you can see it being redrawn, for a moment, when something changes.
- Creatures drawn from DM's own pictures. The one ahead is a large sprite: seen from the front
  it shifts between two frames (the second mirrored, as DM does), and as in DM it shows its
  side, its back or its attack when it faces across the party's view, away from it, or strikes;
  it flashes white when hit. Up to three more, farther off or to the sides, are small sprites.
- Sound effects on the SID (`src/sound.s`), standing in for DM's sampled ones: switches, doors,
  blows, wounds, swings, fireballs and explosions, spells, four kinds of creature cry,
  creatures dying, picking things up, eating and drinking, teleporters and falling.
- Sensors: floor plates (anything, party, object, party carrying an object, facing a
  direction), wall switches, keyholes that keep the key, any-object and specific-object
  sensors, AND/OR gates and countdowns. Effects are set, clear, toggle and hold, with delays,
  once-only and reversed. They open and close doors, pits and teleporters, and show or hide texts.
  The sensor bit layout was worked out from the data (a target's coordinates land on the doors
  it should open, for example). The gates' and countdowns' details are a best guess.
- Doors that slide shut and open over time, door buttons, and doors that won't close on the party.
- Stairs and pits between levels, lined up by each level's place in the dungeon. Teleporters
  move the party, within a level or to another one, with their rotation.
- Recruiting champions from the mirrors, with an inventory of 15 slots each. Objects travel
  with the party from level to level. The inventory is DM's own: its picture in the view's
  place, each object as DM's icon in its slot (the hands, head, neck, body, legs, feet and the
  first eight places in the backpack), the food bar, and the champion's portrait beside it;
  their numbers are in the text below.
- Melee combat using the weapon tables. Creature groups chase and attack at their own speeds,
  and drop what they carry when they die. Weapons pass through non-material creatures (ghosts,
  black flames, materializers, water elementals): only magic, or a Vorpal Blade, hurts them.
- Magic: casting with mana costs and skill checks, and spells as projectiles that fly through
  the view (fireball, lightning, poison bolt and cloud, harm non-material, and ZO, which opens
  doors; fireballs blast open doors that can be burnt), potions cast into empty flasks (all
  nine), party and fire shields, invisibility (creatures stop chasing), and ZOKATHRA.
- A map of each level, showing only what the party has seen: walls, doors, stairs, open pits,
  visible teleporters and objects on the floor. It's kept with the level, so it's saved too.
- Food, health/stamina/mana recovery, potions (VI, MON, EE, ROS, KU, DANE, NETA, water), and
  scrolls.
- Light and darkness, by DM's rules (`src/light.c`): every level but the first is dark, lit
  by torches in the champions' hands (as bright as their charges, burning down as time
  passes), an illumulet, and the light, magic torch and darkness spells, whose light fades
  away step by step. The view darkens through DM's six palettes: each of the C64's colours in
  it becomes, at each level, the C64 colour nearest to what DM shows (`tools/dmview.py`).

### Not yet

- Magic vision, magic footprints, water, experience and levelling up, and poison. Spells can't yet be learnt
  better through practice.
- The dungeon's projectile launchers and creature generators, and creatures casting spells.
- DM's exact formulas for spell damage, shield strength and how long spells last. The ones
  here are simpler stand-ins, scaled by the spell's strength from the table and the power rune.
- Throwing and shooting, bashing doors, creatures using doors and pits, and teleporting objects
  and creatures.
- Creatures in DM's places within a square (a group is one sprite here), stairs seen from the
  side, holes in the ceiling under pits, doors that slide sideways as they open (they all
  slide up here), footprints, DM's champion status boxes (the party is text below the view),
  the rune panel, pouches, the quiver and the rest of the backpack, and DM's own sounds.
- The endgame: the Firestaff, Lord Chaos and the fluxcage.

## How it fits in a C64

```text
$0400-$07FF  buffers (the default screen's RAM)           LOWBSS segment, c64-dm64.cfg
$0801-$BE29  the program, rules tables, the party's level (3.2K buffer), the party's objects
$BE2A-$BF7F  free (about 340 bytes)
$BF80-$C9FF  the overlay area: whichever overlay is in use (2.6K)
$CA00-$CBFF  C stack (512 bytes)
$CC00-$CFFF  the screen; its top 17 rows are the bitmap's colours
$D000-$D3FF  character set             } in the RAM under the I/O area; the video chip uses
$D400-$D6FF  sprites (creatures, from  } bank 3 and always sees RAM there, the CPU writes
             far memory; the pointer)  } with I/O switched out (hw.c: hi_read)
$DC00-$DE3F  DM's inscription font, as bitmap cells
$E000-$FF3F  the bitmap (its top 17 rows: the view, and the panel beside it), in the RAM
             under the KERNAL
far memory   the 14 level images, about 34K (DMLEV), the overlays, 16K (DMOVL), the
             creatures' sprites from every side, 23K (DMSPR), the dungeon's texts, object
             names, our own strings and some rules tables, 8K (DMTXT), and the view's
             pictures, 409K (DMWAL): about 490K of the 512K
```

The screen is split by a raster interrupt (`src/irq.s`): its top 17 rows are a multicolour
bitmap, the rest text. The bitmap's colours share the text screen's memory, so the sprites
have one set of pointers. In the bitmap, every cell has the same background (mid grey) and
the same two other greys (dark and light), and one colour of its own; DM's view is nearly all
greys, so its pictures fit without clashing. Each picture is stored (DMWAL) as the bitmap bytes
of the cells it covers, with masks for the cells it covers only partly, and copied in by
`src/bitmap.s`. That code switches the KERNAL out to reach the bitmap underneath, and
interrupts go on meanwhile: the RAM under the KERNAL's vectors points to a handler that
switches it back in. Objects and spells in flight, which can be anywhere, are stored once per
size and shifted into place a row at a time as they're drawn.

Each level image (see the top of `tools/dmconv.py`) holds the level's squares, the start of
each square's object list, its own tables of doors, teleporters, texts, sensors, creatures
and objects, and a bit for each square the party has seen, for the map. Things are numbered
within the level, so the image can be copied in and out of far memory whole. Objects the party
picks up move into a separate pool (`dungeon.c`), which is how they cross levels.

Code that's only needed now and then lives in **overlays** (`src/overlay.c`): recruiting,
the inventory, help and the map, the casting screen, saving and loading, and unpacking DMWAL
at the start. The linker (`c64-dm64.cfg`) builds each to run in the same 2.6K area, the build
joins them into DMOVL, and the game keeps them in far memory, copying one into the area when
it's called. An overlay can call anything in the main program, but nothing in another overlay.
A new rarely used feature belongs in one. The largest (saving) sets the area's size,
`__OVLSIZE__` in the config. (cc65 writes a file's string literals at its end, into whatever
segment is in force there: so an overlay's file doesn't pop its segments at the end, or its
strings would land in the main program.)

# DTS Parser library
For Commodore Amiga machines running V36 and later OS. 
Provides DTS style hardware configuration files for device and general configuration use.

## Build
Built with SAC/C 6 and smake. Makefile in Src for test code and library build. Makefile in root for supporting header files for library.
TO_DO: VBCC compatible build and alternative make tool outside of SAS/C.
fd2pragma required to build headers. Uses Aminet version https://aminet.net/package/dev/misc/fd2pragma

To build all executable binaries then enter the Src/ dirtory and run
> smake

## Capability
Not everything from all DTS specs will be in this parser due to some custom capabilities not referenced in v0.4 specification.

Some info to note on implementation:
* No DTB is compiled by this implementation. The DTS is parsed and available in memory to query, skipping any conversion to DTB
* Multiline byte arrays and property arrays with comments supported within values 
* Strings interpreted on single lines within quotes
* Property arrays and arrays of u32 values are stored in arrays of Tag Items to handle values which are references
* References to paths are stored as u32 property arrays and therefore Tag Items (singular entry with TAG_END closure)
* Strings are char arrays
* Implementation has a top level node to contain root node, properties and directives/commands. This has no name and no parent node.
* /Include/ directives/commands can be in any node and will load additional file data
* /Include/ files can be called anything. No checks on extensions. This also applies to main DTS file.
* A node with a phandle doesn't need to be defined before it is used in the DTS. The parser will bind references later. Note that missing references could be left hanging (NULL).
* Mixing path and alias/label references, ahead of the actual node with phandle, will create 2 references in memory. Note that both are maintained, but returned ref addresses are different
* Pretty dumb with regards to known property types. Only phandle processed to record a reference
* No formatting checks (see above as parser dumb to known properties) so a value can be set to anything in a property
* No checking for /dts-v1/ directive. User code can still check for it, but parser does not enforce and assumes DTS format
* Parser doesn't treat unrecognised directives/commands as an error. Will continue processing.
* In general the parser isn't very strict and will try to read data as much as possible until it really can't go further. This may create odd results if DTS is not well formatted.
* Overlays with label references or path references supported (similar to Zephyr DTS). Path or node label must exist prior to creating overlay node (cannot forward reference)

## Limitations
* Arithmetic, bitwise or logical expressions in property values (literal string saved as property value but not processed, parser fails if arithmetic in values)
* Max 300 chars for any parsed parameter (changeable in code, but more memory will be used)
* Labels within values (limited purpose and seems useless as not referenced)

Custom DTS capabilities outside of v0.4:
* MACROS are not implemented (no #define, #ifdef, #else, etc)
* #include directives are not used. Use /include/ directive format from v0.4 spec

## Installation
The library is called dts.library and should be installed in LIBS: for general running.
DTS files must be installed to ENVARC: and there must be at least an 'amiga.dts' file in that directory.
There are example DTS files in the DTS/ directory.
> Type smake install from the root build directory to install to ENVARC:

## Running
The first instance to open the library will invoke the parser and create a DTS representation in memory.
If there are any errors then the library will fail to open. Check your files for errors and try again.
There is an test file called 'dtstest' which takes a DTS file as a parameter. Run the following will give output or a line error:
> dtstest ENVARC:amiga.dts

The library will remain in memory with a cache of the DTS. This means that any changes will not be parsed until the library is closed and reinitialised.
In the Amiga OS the library can be closed and released from memory with a call to
>avail flush

All instances of the library must be closed to free (meaning that no processes are using the library). Last resort is a reboot. 

### DTS files
DTS files exist in the DTS/ directory. Copying all to ENVARC: creates an example environment.
DTS entries should be configured to match the actual environment in-use. Examples include a base A500 Rev 6 and A1200 representation. 
All DTS files should overlay from the base A500 version and provide additional hardware. This is done in the 'amiga.dts' which manages this through /include/ directives.
To add or remove a definition then the best practice is to add or remove the /include/ in the 'amiga.dts' and leave the dtsi files as they were in ENVARC. Additional hardware or changes to base hardware can then be added to the 'amiga.dts' directly or added to another dtsi file and included at the end of the include directives. 
Note that all include references must be full paths.

### Library examples
An example file, 'Src/libtest.c' shows how to open the library and run some of the API commands. 
The example covers what most drivers would want to query from the DTS with a compatibility search and address information queried.

### About WinAGI:  

WinAGI is a full featured game development system, that includes editors which provide full control over of all resources in an AGI game. It includes several integrated tools to assist in game design and development, allowing you to create new AGI games more efficiently and with less effort. 

WinAGI GDS v3 represents a completely rewritten/refreshed codebase (based on the original VB6 version) with an updated project structure and a clean repository history. All capabilities of the last VB release (v2.3.7) are fully supported, and many new enhancements and additions are included.

Game projects created in v2 can be opened in this version, and the WAG file and source files will be automatically updated. Note that game projects in v3 are not backward compatible and cannot be opened in v2.

The Help file included with this release contains detailed information on all the features and tools available.

This is a beta release. Feedback, bug reports, and feature requests are welcome.

# ![ROTH.C banner](images/ROTH.C_banner.png)

**ROTH.C, a native recreation of `ROTH.EXE`, the engine of _Realms of the Haunting_ (1996), as verified,
readable C, with a built-in modding platform.**

_Realms of the Haunting_ shipped as a DOS program. ROTH.C is that program's engine, reconstructed
function by function into C that has been verified against the original executable's behavior, then
wrapped in a native host (SDL3) so it runs as an ordinary desktop application: windowed, with
working mouse capture, music, and sound. No DOSBox required!

The game's content is not included; you simply take a couple files from this project and drop it
into your existing Realms of the Haunting installation folder and you can play.

## ![Playing banner](images/ROTH.C_playing_banner.png)

1. Download the latest [Release](https://github.com/beyond-the-ire/ROTH.C/releases/latest) for your system (Windows or Linux).
   - **Windows:** `rothc.exe` (the engine), `SDL3.dll`, `gm.sf2` (soundfont), and an empty `mods/` folder.
   - **Linux:** `roth` (the engine), `libSDL3.so.0`, `gm.sf2` (soundfont), and an empty `mods/` folder.
2. Extract everything into your installation's `ROTH` directory. (this is the one containing `CONFIG.INI` and
   the game's data files, which is `"Realms of the Haunting/ROTH/"` in the Steam version).
3. Double click `rothc.exe` (for Windows) or `roth` (for Linux). You can also run either from the commandline for logging.

**Note on the Windows name:** the executable is `rothc.exe` rather than `roth.exe` on purpose —
Windows filenames are case-insensitive, so `roth.exe` would overwrite the original `ROTH.EXE`
sitting in the same folder.

**Note on MIDI:** Since the original game uses MIDI music and relied on a physical sound card back in the day, this native
version of the game relies on using a soundfont to determine how to play the MIDI tracks in the game.
This is the reason why `gm.sf2` needs to be copied over as well. This also means that you're free
to use your own soundfont without needing specialized MIDI-playing software.

## ![System banner](images/ROTH.C_system_banner.png)

Linux x86 and Windows are supported. The engine is a 32-bit program by nature, which is kept
preserved, so the Linux build requires 32-bit runtime libraries (the release bundles its own
SDL3), and the Windows build is a 32-bit executable that runs as-is on 64-bit Windows (the
release bundles its own `SDL3.dll`; no other runtime is needed).

## ![Mods banner](images/ROTH.C_mods_banner.png)

> First-party mods can be found here: [`roth-mods`](https://github.com/beyond-the-ire/roth-mods)

ROTH.C ships with built-in modding infrastructure, allowing mods to be added very easily. Simply create a `mods/` folder
in the installation directory (see step 2 under the Playing section above) and drop the mods you want into it.

Mods themselves are just folders with a few files in them. See [Modding](#modding) for more information.

## ![Building from source banner](images/ROTH.C_build_banner.png)

### On Linux

Prerequisites: `gcc` with 32-bit multilib support, GNU `make`, `python3`, binutils, and the 32-bit
SDL3 build (fetches a pinned SDL release; needs `cmake`, `git`, network access,
and your distribution's 32-bit X11/ALSA/PipeWire/Mesa client libraries):

```
tools/build_sdl3_i386.sh        # one-time: builds roth_c/third_party/sdl3-i386
make -C sdk check               # the SDK's consistency gates (should print ALL GATES PASS)
make -C roth_c                  # the moddable engine + the dev viewer
make -C roth_c dist             # assemble the release bundle into roth_c/dist/
```

See [`roth_c/README.md`](roth_c/README.md) for build details, run options, and the development
tools.

### The two build flavors

- **moddable** (the default, what releases ship): carries the runtime plugin platform — a loader
  for mod plugins and inert padding at every engine function that lets mods override engine
  behavior at startup. With no mods installed, the engine verifies at boot that every pad is
  untouched.
- **vanilla** (`make -C roth_c FLAVOR=vanilla`): no mod surface at all — no loader, no padding.
  Mods are impossible by construction. The reference artifact for anyone who wants the
  reconstruction and nothing else.

### The Windows build

The Windows executable is cross-compiled from Linux with the MinGW i686 toolchain
(`gcc-mingw-w64-i686` on Debian/Ubuntu):

```
tools/build_sdl3_win32.sh              # one-time: builds roth_c/third_party/sdl3-win32
make -C roth_c CROSS=mingw             # the moddable Windows engine (rothc.exe)
make -C roth_c CROSS=mingw dist-win    # assemble the Windows bundle into roth_c/dist-win/
```

`CROSS=mingw` composes with everything above (`FLAVOR=vanilla` included), and the Windows link
runs additional post-link gates of its own — including one that asserts the executable's memory
layout, which the engine's fixed-address data depends on. Details in
[`roth_c/README.md`](roth_c/README.md).

## ![Modding banner](images/ROTH.C_modding_banner.png)

ROTH.C is built to be modded. Mods are native plugins loaded at startup from `mods/<name>/` —
users install them by extracting a folder, and remove them by deleting it. A mod can patch game
data at boot, remap keys, watch and rewrite input, draw overlays on every frame, call engine
functions, and wrap or replace individual engine functions. The engine's reconstructed source
makes "copy the real function, modify it, override it" a first-class technique.

Useful switches: `--no-mods` (start with the mod platform inert), `--list-mods` (show what would load and
exit), `--scale N` (initial window scale). The full list is in
[`roth_c/README.md`](roth_c/README.md).

- **Writing mods**: start with [`sdk/MODDING_GUIDE.md`](sdk/MODDING_GUIDE.md) — the mod types,
  the execution-context rules, the override chain semantics, and a build recipe. The SDK's
  machinery (schemas, generated headers, ABI gates) is documented in
  [`sdk/README.md`](sdk/README.md). Two minimal teaching examples live in `sdk/examples/`.
- **Ready-made mods**: the companion repository
  [`roth-mods`](https://github.com/beyond-the-ire/roth-mods) hosts downloadable mods (key
  rebinding, an item browser, an enlarged document viewer, …), each a drop-in folder.

## ![Repository layout banner](images/ROTH.C_repository_banner.png)

| path                   | contents                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `roth_c/src/engine/`   | the reconstructed game engine (see the note below)                                                           |
| `roth_c/src/data/`     | the engine's reconstructed static data, as named, typed C                                                    |
| `roth_c/src/platform/` | the native host: video/input/audio (SDL3), the DOS-era OS services the engine expects, the mod plugin loader |
| `sdk/`                 | the modding SDK: schemas, generated headers, ABI baselines, the guide, teaching examples                     |
| `tools/`               | the SDK generators/validators and the SDL3 build script                                                      |
| `docs/reference/`      | machine-readable reference data the SDK tooling consumes                                                     |

## ![Fidelity banner](images/ROTH.C_fidelity_banner.png)

`roth_c/src/engine/` is a **preservation artifact**. It reproduces the original engine's behavior (+ its quirks)
with every function verified against the original executable, at the
level of instructions and bytes, before it was accepted. It is deliberately not "improved":
faithful reconstruction is the point, and it is what makes the source trustworthy as
documentation of how the game actually works.

Consequences worth knowing:

- Bugs that existed in the original are preserved (unless they crash; a handful of provable
  original niche defects are guarded in the moddable build only, each documented at the site with the
  original's disassembly).
- Enhancements do not go into the engine. They belong in either the platform layer or as mods.
- Changes to the engine source are accepted only as _fidelity fixes_: corrections that bring the
  C closer to the original's actual behavior, with evidence. See
  [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md).

## ![Credits banner](images/ROTH.C_credits_banner.png)

- **_Realms of the Haunting_** was developed by **Gremlin Interactive** (1996). This project is a
  fan reconstruction and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to the game's
  developers, publishers, or rights holders. All trademarks belong to their owners.
- The bundled soundfont is **GeneralUser GS** by S. Christian Collins.
- Built with **SDL 3** and **TinySoundFont**.

## ![License banner](images/ROTH.C_license_banner.png)

Two-part (see [`LICENSE`](LICENSE) for the full text):

- **The reconstructed engine** (`roth_c/src/engine/`, `roth_c/src/data/`, `docs/reference/`) is
  published as a preservation notice: provided for preservation, study, and interoperability;
  the underlying game's rights remain entirely with its rights holders, and rights-holder
  concerns will be addressed promptly and in good faith.
- **The original work** (the platform layer, the SDK, the tooling, the documentation) is
  **MIT-licensed**, meaning mods built against the SDK may be distributed freely.

No game assets are included in this repository or its releases; the original game files must be
obtained from a lawfully acquired copy of the game, such as from [GOG](https://www.gog.com/en/game/realms_of_the_haunting)
or [Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/292390/Realms_of_the_Haunting/).

# Van der Bijl historic code archive

This repository preserves a curated collection of DOS-era source code and school work written circa 1987–1997. The collection includes BASIC and Turbo Pascal programs published under the RobSoft and R&L names, the SO_NEW vocabulary program, the TAP time-administration program, the RMS timetable-change manager, and later data-acquisition, PLC, robotics, machine-vision, timer, control, and signal-processing work.

The archive is historical, not a maintained software distribution. Original standalone source files are retained byte-for-byte. Source recovered from contemporary printed listings is identified in the file header. OCR corrections, reconstructed text and missing dependencies are documented alongside the recovered files; the accompanying scans retain the historical evidence.

## Highlights

| Location | Approximate date | Content | Attribution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| tap/ | 1989 | TAP 4.0, a DOS time-administration application | Co-written by Robbert van der Bijl and Lars Kemper; R & L Productions |
| so-new/ | 1990s | SO_NEW source states, including registered version 1.2, annotated listing, feedback, and upgrade/serial-number documents | R & L Productions; supporting documents name Robbert van der Bijl as author/contact |
| rms/ | 1994 | RMS 0.10 beta timetable-change management source and original listing | R & L Productions |
| basic/unattributed/gedachtenlezen/ | Undated | Short BASIC number-guessing game and original listing | Unconfirmed |
| pascal/ | 1987–1988 | Turbo Pascal games, graphics, sound, interface experiments, and exercises | Robbert/RobSoft where identified; DOBBEL.PAS and GER1.PAS by Gerrit van der Bijl |
| basic/robsoft/ | 1989 | PC-speaker music-board program | RobSoft |
| dos/so-plus/ | 1988 | DOS boot-disk installation batch program | RobSoft |
| school/ | 1995–1997 | PCL-1800 DAQ, 8254 timer, PLC, SCARA/PUMA robotics, machine vision, digital control, and FFT source | Robbert van der Bijl and Jeroen Eikmans where credited in the source headers |

See [CATALOG.md](CATALOG.md) for what the programs do, [AUTHORS.md](AUTHORS.md) for attribution, and [PROVENANCE.md](PROVENANCE.md) for provenance details.

## File formats

Several retained sources use DOS line endings, a DOS end-of-file marker, or an OEM character set, so browser rendering may differ from the original DOS display.

## Rights

This material is published for historical preservation and study. Copyright and other rights remain with the respective authors. No general open-source license or permission for commercial reuse is asserted by this repository. Copyright notices and attributions embedded in the original files remain authoritative.

# DMMac: Dungeon Master for macOS and Windows DMMac is a native C11 and SDL3 port of the Amiga versions of **Dungeon Master v3.60** and **Chaos Strikes Back** for macOS (Apple Silicon) and Windows (x86-64).

This repository contains no game data. You must provide your own Amiga disk images (`.adf`): Dungeon Master v3.60 (1 disk) and optionally Chaos Strikes Back (disks A and B). DOS, Atari ST, and other Amiga releases are not supported. The game identifies a disk by its content, not by its file name. ## Features - **Full campaigns:** Both Dungeon Master and Chaos Strikes Back are playable to the end. - **Vanilla mode:** The original rules, timing, and interface. - **Advanced mode:** Automap, in-game options menu (volume, music, upscale filter), 8 save slots, quick save/load, cheat screen, WASD movement, 8 simultaneous sounds, FM-Towns and Super NES soundtracks, and direct entry to Chaos Strikes Back from the prison stairs. - **LLM mode (macOS only, `--mode turnbased`):** A program plays the game turn by turn over a Unix socket. - **Display scaling:** Window resizing with the `scale2x` and `scale3x` pixel-art filters. ## Play Download the [latest release](https://github.com/peterkmet/dmmac/releases/latest) (`DMMac-macos-arm64.zip` or `DMMac-windows-x64.zip`), extract it, and copy your `.adf` disk images into the folder. - **macOS:** Remove the quarantine attribute and launch `Dungeon Master.command` (or double-click it in Finder): ```sh xattr -d com.apple.quarantine dm "Dungeon Master.command" libSDL3.0.dylib open "Dungeon Master.command" ``` - **Windows 10+:** Run `dm.exe`. If Windows SmartScreen warns about an unknown publisher, select "More info", then "Run anyway". On first launch, the game extracts the disk images into `game/` and `game-csb/`. Each adventure keeps its saves in its own folder, in the original Amiga format. Keys of the advanced mode (in the dungeon view): | Key | Action | |---|---| | W, A, S, D, Q, E | Move and turn | | M, Tab | Automap | | Escape | Options menu | | C | Cheat screen | | F5, F9 | Quick save, quick load | | Ctrl+S | Save dialog with the 8 slots | See the [Player manual](docs/manual.md) for all controls, game modes, and configuration. ## Let an LLM play ```sh build/dm --mode turnbased --control /tmp/dm.sock DM_CONTROL=/tmp/dm.sock uv run dm-play --brief get_state DM_CONTROL=/tmp/dm.sock uv run dm-play act move_forward ``` The `dm-mcp` server exposes the control socket over the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for clients such as Claude Code. [LLM mode: turn-based play over MCP](docs/llm/llm-mode.md) has the protocol, the actions, and the setup. [LLM runs](docs/llm/llm-runs.md) describes playthroughs with a coordinator and player agents. ## Build ```sh brew install sdl3 uv sync make # Build build/dm and the test library make test # Run the test suite make check # Check formatting, coding standard, and tests make windows # Cross-compile build/dm.exe with MinGW-w64 ``` Run `build/dm` from the folder with your `.adf` images. See [Development](docs/development.md) for build and release workflows, [Architecture](docs/architecture.md) and [Coding standard](docs/coding-standard.md) for codebase structure, and [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md) for release history. ## Engineering Claude Code built the port in four stages: 1. **Decompilation:** Ghidra decompiled the 68000 FTL modules to C ([Decompiling](docs/decompiling.md)). The symbol tables in `docs/reference/` name the functions and globals. 2. **Reimplementation:** Claude Code rewrote the game logic in C11 from the decompilation alone, without code from other ports. 3. **Differential verification:** Automated tests run each ported C function and the original 68000 code in an emulator with the same input and compare the state. Golden snapshots validate save files, viewport rendering, and game mechanics. 4. **Refactoring:** Later passes added named constants, typed accessors, the five layers, and the automated coding-standard checks. The game behavior did not change. DMMac takes only the function and structure names from [ReDMCSB](http://dmweb.free.fr/community/redmcsb/), Christophe Fontanel's reconstruction of the original 68000 source, so the two code bases are easy to compare. More: [FTL module format](docs/formats/ftl.md), [Game state](docs/rules/game-state.md), [Chaos Strikes Back data files](docs/csb/data.md), [KAOS module map](docs/reference/kaos-map.md). ## Acknowledgements - [SDL3](https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL) — windowing, input, and audio output. - [dr_mp3](https://github.com/mackron/dr_libs) by David Reid — MP3 audio decoding. - [amitools](https://github.com/cnvogelg/amitools) — ADF image extraction and reference implementation for ADF reader tests. - [machine68k](https://github.com/cnvogelg/machine68k) — 68000 CPU emulation for differential tests. - [ReDMCSB](http://dmweb.free.fr/community/redmcsb/) by Christophe Fontanel — symbol and structure naming reference. - [dmcsb](https://codeberg.org/CyCl0ne/DungeonMasterTools) by Cycl0ne — reference validator for the `Dungeon.DAT` tests. ## License GPL-3.0-or-later ([LICENSE](LICENSE)). Dungeon Master and Chaos Strikes Back are properties of FTL Games. This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by the rights holders. Original game data is not included and is not covered by this license.

# Krypton Egg An Android remake of **Krypton Egg**, the Breakout game by Alexandre Kral (Atari ST and Amiga, 1989) in its Windows CD version published by C2V in 1996. You move a racket along the bottom of the screen and bounce a ball into walls of bricks. Catch the spells that fall out of broken bricks, and shoot or dodge the monsters that come through the door at the top. **No ads, no in-app purchases, no analytics.**


Level 1: bricks on a teal floor between wooden walls, the racket and ball at the bottom.

## Download **Direct APK download:** https://github.com/Matswm86/krypton-egg/releases/download/latest/krypton-egg.apk 1. Open that link in your phone's browser and download the file. 2. Open the downloaded file. If Android says it is not allowed to install unknown apps from this source, tap **Settings**, turn on **Allow from this source**, go back and install. 3. The app appears as **Krypton Egg** and runs in landscape. The APK is debug-signed with a fixed key, so a newer build installs over an older one. ## What it does - Play all 100 levels, in 10 worlds of 10; each world you finish unlocks on the PLAY menu. - Slide a finger anywhere on the screen to steer the racket, and tap to launch the ball or fire. - Break plain, multi-hit, framed, stone, metal and exploding bricks, and catch the 18 spells that fall from them: longer racket, laser, shield, fire ball and more. - Shoot or dodge the monsters that come through the door at the top. - Put your name in the top-5 high-score table, which is kept on the phone. - Watch the original cutscenes and read the INFO pages that explain the spells and the enemies. ## How it works The game is written in GDScript for Godot 4.6 and drawn with the GL Compatibility renderer at the original 320 x 200 resolution, which the engine scales up to the phone screen. Python tools in `tools/` decode the original resource file from the CD into PNG sprite sheets, WAV samples, the level data and the FLI cutscenes, and the game loads those files directly. A small FLI player decodes the cutscene animations frame by frame and a palette shader colours them. The brick, spell and monster rules are my own GDScript, written from the sprites and the original help text. GitHub Actions exports the debug APK with Godot 4.6.2 and publishes it as the rolling `latest` release. ## Status Version 0.1.0, playable from level 1 to level 100. Not done yet: the horde-attack stages, the final-monster battles and three of the eight cutscenes. ## Controls - **Slide a finger** anywhere on the screen to move the racket. The racket follows the finger's movement, like a mouse, so your finger never covers it. - **Tap** to launch the ball, and to fire when the racket carries a laser or a cannon. - **Back** pauses the game. Back again while paused returns to the menu. - On a keyboard: left and right arrows move, space launches, Escape pauses. ## What comes from the original Everything you see and hear was decoded from the original game files on the *C2V Games Suite* CD (1996), preserved on [archive.org](https://archive.org/details/c2v-game-suite): - **All 100 levels**, byte for byte, including each level's ball speed and its list of monster types. - **All graphics**: 256 brick sprites, 66 monster frames, 49 racket frames, 90 spell and ball frames, the floor tiles, the wooden walls, the score panels, the menu, the title picture and the high-score picture. - **All 45 sound effects** and the music: title, menu, scores, info, pause, game over, and the CD soundtrack pieces that play under the cutscenes. - **Five of the eight cutscenes** (320 x 200 FLI animations): the C2V logo, the space-ship intro, the racket flying into the playfield when a game starts, and the flight between planets after every 10 levels. The last level ends with the planet explosion. The tunnel, zoom and spinning-racket clips are baked into the APK but not placed yet. The game uses the original 320 x 200 screen and the original playfield layout, scaled up to fill the phone's height. ## What I had to decide The CD does not describe what each brick and spell does; that logic lives in the 16-bit program code. These rules are my reading of the sprites, the sound names and the original help text, not a port of the original code: - **Bricks.** Plain bricks break in one hit. Bricks with one to three blue plus marks need that many extra hits. Framed bricks lose the frame on the first hit. Cracked stone needs two hits. The grey and greek-key metal frames do not count toward clearing the stage and break after six hits, so no stage can lock up. Checkered and flame bricks explode and take their neighbours with them. - **Spells.** 18 spells, each drawn with its original icon: longer racket, shorter racket, glue, multiple ball, bigger ball, fire ball, laser, cannon, slow ball, fast ball, frozen tray, shield, dynamite, fly, mystery, extra racket, reversed controls and small ball. The INFO screen lists them with their icons. - **Monsters** follow the original rule from the help text: you can touch most of them, but the picus vulgarus kills a racket that has no shield. - **Worlds.** Every 10 levels finished unlocks that world on the PLAY menu, in place of the original's passwords. Not in this version yet: the horde-attack stages and the final-monster battles. Their graphics and music are on the CD, but how they played has to be rebuilt from scratch. ## Building The APK is built by GitHub Actions (`.github/workflows/build-android.yml`) with Godot 4.6.2. To rebuild the assets from the CD yourself: ```sh # 1. Unpack KRYPTON/COM/CDROM/KE.RSC from the CD image, then: python3 tools/carve_cd.py KE.RSC /tmp/ke python3 tools/bake_assets.py /tmp/ke ``` `tools/carve_cd.py` splits the resource file (most of it is stored with every byte inverted), `tools/gaf.py` and `tools/dig.py` decode C2V's GAF sprite and sample banks, and `scripts/fli_player.gd` plays the FLI cutscenes on the phone. Krypton Egg is © Alexandre Kral and C2V. This is a fan remake for people who played it on Windows in the nineties.

# Lotus Turbo Challenge 2 — native

A native port of *Lotus Turbo Challenge 2* (Amiga CD32 / AGA, 1991,
Magnetic Fields / Gremlin Graphics).

The shipped binary contains **no emulator**.  The game's 68000 code is
statically recompiled to C ahead of time, and a growing set of routines
has been replaced outright by hand-written native C.  `make no-musashi`
is a build gate that fails if a single emulator symbol reaches the
native executable.

```
./run.sh         # build it and play it
./run.sh debug   # ...starting on the course preview instead
```

One binary: the game with its bezel, and the RE pages a button away.  X
swaps between them, on the keyboard or the pad.  `make play` and `make
debug` do the same thing.

You supply the game.  The retail WHDLoad install lives in
`original/Lotus2CD32/` and is never committed — see *Legal* below.

## How it is built

**The recompiler.**  `tools/m68k2c.py` turns 68000 into C: one `switch`
over the program counter, over a machine struct.  It decodes from the
PCs a real run actually executed, then follows the code by recursive
descent and through jump tables, so the instruction boundaries are
observed rather than guessed.  Cycle costs are measured per EDGE (this
PC to that next PC) from the oracle's own counter, not averaged per
instruction — the difference matters, because the game's interrupt
timing depends on it.

**The oracle.**  Musashi runs the same game beside it and produces
entry/exit RAM and register images.  It is a measuring instrument only;
nothing from `third_party/musashi/` is linked into the native build.

**The gates.**  Nothing is accepted because it looks right.

| gate | what it demands |
| --- | --- |
| `make recomp-gate` | 28 recompiled routines, register- and memory-exact against the oracle |
| `make frame-gate` | 30 checkpoints through a full boot-and-race, pixel-identical |
| `make render-gate` | the native compositor's frame appears verbatim inside the oracle's raster |
| `make course-gate` | all eight courses reached and compared |
| `make override-check` | whether a routine may be replaced at all: entered only by BSR/JSR, and every register it changes reproduced |
| `make no-musashi` | no emulator symbols in the native binary |

**The engine.**  `src/engine/` is the ported game: the road pipeline
(sky bands, keyframe generator, edge interpolator, perspective pass,
blit queue, band blitter), the car model, the input decoder, a blitter,
and a per-line copper compositor.  Each routine carries the address it
came from and the snapshot that proves it.

## The RE pages

`make debug` gives the game plus five pages.  The COURSE page runs the
game's own road chain over a race snapshot and seeks it by writing the
course position long at `$30d8(A3)` — the same record index the game's
generator walks the course table by — so dragging the scrub bar drives
the real interpolator, beside a top-down map, a gradient profile and a
whole-course strip read from the same table.

## Some things learned the hard way

* `move.w` leaves the top half of a data register alone; an address
  register as destination is always 32-bit and sets no flags.  One
  `addq.w #6,A0` treated as a word cost five gates.
* `asr` is arithmetic.  Implemented as a logical shift on an unsigned
  value it drops every other bit, and the oracle diff looks like
  `expected AND $55`.
* A read-modify-write through `(An)+` adjusts the pointer once, not
  twice.
* Decode images must be coherent per memory region.  A stale chip-RAM
  image still disassembles — into confident nonsense.
* A routine can be byte-exact and still not be replaceable.  Charging a
  fixed cycle cost for a routine whose real cost varies per course
  (`car_update`: 970 cycles in FOREST, 768 in STORM) breaks the frames
  it used to pass.

## Layout

```
src/host/      chipset, WHDLoad shim, front ends
src/recomp/    generated C + the runtime it runs on
src/engine/    routines ported to native C
src/viewer/    the RE pages
tools/         recompiler, gates, capture and analysis
re/            what the reverse engineering found
third_party/   Musashi (oracle only)
```

## Legal

The code here is mine.  The game is not.  The retail slave, `Disk.1` and
everything extracted from them stay out of this repository; `.gitignore`
enforces it.  Bring your own copy.
