# ANVIL

**ANVIL** is an algorithmic MIDI composition instrument for the browser. You set rules; ANVIL
composes short themes from them, makes variations, and plays them through up to six voices of
accompaniment derived from the theme, on your MIDI hardware, its own small synthesiser, or
samples you load. It can render what it plays to WAV files and sample-aligned stems.

The name follows a line of descent: Tunesmith → smith → anvil.

## Inspiration, and what ANVIL is not

ANVIL is inspired by **Dr. T's Tunesmith** (Jim Johnson, Dr. T's Music Software, 1988-91), an
Atari ST program that generated themes and variations from rhythmic "microrhythms", weighted
scale degrees and step/leap rules, and derived accompaniments from them.

ANVIL is **not** a port, emulator or copy of Tunesmith. It contains none of its code,
graphics, text, presets or data, and its interface is its own. Its Classic mode reconstructs
the original's documented and observed *behaviour*; where that behaviour is unknown, ANVIL's
own approximations are labelled, documented and versioned. ANVIL is not affiliated with or
endorsed by Jim Johnson or Dr. T's Music Software (see [NOTICE.md](NOTICE.md)).

ANVIL belongs to a small collection of instruments alongside **emmm** (after Intelligent
Music's M), **FrakMC** (Fractal Music Composer) and **Feelers** (after Dr. T's Fingers /
MIDI-AX), and shares their visual family and palette names.

## Classic and Extended

- **Classic**: the reconstruction. Five themes x three variations, six rhythm algorithms,
  weighted pitch rules, five rhythm and four pitch variation algorithms, 38 + 8 scales, six
  voices with 12 rhythms, Divide, 11 harmonies and 5 drum algorithms, 8 articulations,
  26 + 26 presets, arranger. Fully usable on its own.
- **Extended**: the same engine with new tools: regenerate only rhythm, pitches or accents,
  lock notes, keep contour, mutate, type seeds, compare items, see ancestry.

Projects remember their mode. Switching never changes the music.

## The system in brief

1. **Constraints**: rhythm (microbeat, length, pulse, rest %, algorithm, variant), pitch
   (first note, loop, low/high, max step/leap/repeats, onbeat/offbeat weight tables) and
   variation (rhythm var, pitch var, V).
2. **Themes & variations**: click a slot to play it (generating it if empty); G, double-click
   or right-click regenerates. Variations are made from their row's theme.
3. **Theme view**: see the structure (pulses, microrhythm cells, accents) and edit notes:
   drag notes for pitch and timing, drag a right edge for length, Backspace deletes,
   double-click a rest to add a note; wheel and swipe to scroll, Ctrl/Cmd+wheel to zoom.
   EXPAND opens a maximised editor window (roll, edit buttons, status line); RESTORE or
   Esc returns to the normal layout.
4. **Tonality**: scale, mode, key, octave, user scales, weight tables, drum table.
5. **Accompaniment**: voices 2-6 take rhythm, divide and harmony from the theme.
6. **Arranger**: a list of steps with durations; can be recorded live.

Full behaviour, with evidence for each rule: [docs/BEHAVIOUR.md](docs/BEHAVIOUR.md).

## Internal audio, samples and export

ANVIL always sends MIDI. It can also play its own **internal audio** in the browser (AUDIO tab,
INTERNAL AUDIO): a small synthesiser, or samples.

- **Sample Bank** (SAMPLES, top right): thirteen slots, V1-V6 for the six voices and D1-D7 for
  the seven drum-table entries, so a drum voice can play a different sample per drum-table
  entry. Load or drop WAV, AIFF, MP3, OGG, FLAC, M4A... Each slot has a root note (chromatic
  playback-rate transposition, like a hardware sampler), tune, fine, volume, pan, velocity
  sensitivity, ONE SHOT / GATED / LOOP, start/end and loop points, release, mute and audition.
  A voice set to SAMPLE plays the internal synth wherever its slot is empty.
- **Sample transformations** rework a sample once with The Good Bits' STRETCH FX chain (its
  stretch characters, varispeed pitch, reverse, drive, crunch), keeping the original.
- **Output engine** (AUDIO tab): The Good Bits' output processing per voice and on the master:
  output-stage characters, drive, crunch (bit depth and sample-rate reduction), gain and tone,
  with presets such as 12-BIT and a bypass. CLEAN leaves the sound exactly as it was.
- **Export audio** (EXPORT, top right): an item (a theme or variation, N passes) or the
  arrangement, exactly as START or PLAY ARRANGER plays it, to a master WAV, one stem per voice,
  or both (one ZIP). 44.1 kHz, 16-bit, stereo; every file starts at the same sample with the
  same length; no trimming or normalising. Stems carry their voice's processing; master
  processing is applied to the master only (summing the stems gives the mix before master
  processing).
- Samples stay in this browser (IndexedDB) and survive reloads. **DOWNLOAD BUNDLE** writes a
  portable `.anvilpack` with the project and its samples.

External MIDI instruments cannot be rendered by the browser: record them separately. Details:
[docs/USER-GUIDE.md](docs/USER-GUIDE.md) and
[docs/SAMPLE-AUDIO-ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/SAMPLE-AUDIO-ARCHITECTURE.md).

## Slop Factory Core

ANVIL's audio, sampling, processing, rendering, export and storage come from **Slop Factory
Core** (`@slopfactory/core`, <https://github.com/clickysteve/slopfactory-core>), the shared audio
package of the instruments in the collection; DOWNBEAT uses the same version. It was first built
here and now lives in its own repository; ANVIL installs a version tag of it and bundles it into
its static build. Core reuses The Good Bits' DSP verbatim and knows nothing about ANVIL. See
[docs/SLOP-FACTORY-CORE.md](docs/SLOP-FACTORY-CORE.md).

## MIDI setup

Use Chrome, Edge, Opera or Firefox (Web MIDI; ANVIL never asks for SysEx). In the **MIDI**
tab choose an **Output**; set each voice's channel in the accompaniment table. Without MIDI,
switch on **Audio preview** (the same switch as INTERNAL AUDIO in the AUDIO tab). The MIDI monitor shows traffic in and out; MIDI clock is
summarised as a rate rather than listed.

### Internal clock (ANVIL as master)

Set the tempo; switch on **CLOCK OUT** to send MIDI clock (24 per quarter note) with Start,
Continue and Stop. Clock can go to the note output or another port ("Clock to").

### External clock (ANVIL as slave)

Choose the **Input** in the MIDI tab and set **CLOCK** to External. ANVIL advances exactly one
step per received clock and follows Start (from the top), Continue (from where it stopped) and
Stop (pause in place). Clock alone never starts playback. If clock stops arriving, ANVIL shows
**CLOCK LOST**, ends its notes and waits for Start/Continue from the master or your CONTINUE.
Clock out is off while following external clock.

### Squarp Hermod+

The **Hermod+ setup** demo puts voices 1-4 on channels 1-4 with Clock Out on. As master:
connect by USB, choose the Hermod+ as output, set the Hermod+ to follow USB clock. As slave:
set the Hermod+ to send clock over USB, choose it as input and set Clock to External. This
setup has **not** been verified on hardware by the developers.

## Transport

| Control | Key | Does |
|---|---|---|
| START | Space (when not playing), Return (when stopped) | play from the beginning |
| PAUSE | Return (while playing) | stop in place |
| CONTINUE | Return (while paused) | resume from where it paused |
| STOP/RESET | Space (while playing), Esc | stop and return to the beginning |
| ONCE | | play the theme once |
| END | | stop at the end of the current theme |
| PANIC | Shift+Esc | silence every note on every channel |

## Saving

Work autosaves in the browser. **Save in browser** keeps named copies; **Download** writes a
`.anvil.json` file; **Open file** reads one back (older formats are upgraded, damaged values
repaired with a report). Project files refer to samples but never contain audio; **Download
bundle** writes an `.anvilpack` with the samples, which Open file also reads. **Export item /
arranger** writes a Standard MIDI File of exactly what ANVIL plays. Palettes and MIDI port
choices are browser preferences, not project data.

Project format 2 adds the audio settings. Format 1 projects open unchanged (every voice on
the internal synth, no processing); older versions of ANVIL refuse format 2 files.

## Palettes

Classic (black on white), Dark and Colour, plus custom palettes made by editing any colour in
the **Look** tab. Colours are semantic roles (each panel area has its own ink).

## Known limitations

Not implemented (none of these block normal use):

- the original's occasional large pitch jumps (their trigger is unknown, so they are not reproduced);
- arranger overdub (Record replaces the step list);
- master fade in/out, metronome;
- MIDI control input (changing tonality or items from a keyboard);
- Song Position Pointer (sent or received), clock thru;
- MIDI file import.
- audio export starts from START or PLAY ARRANGER: changes made by hand during a performance
  are not rendered; there are no choke groups or multi-sample instruments; Chromium may move
  individual exported samples by one 16-bit step between two renders of the same project.

MIDI timing in the browser: ANVIL schedules up to 100 ms ahead and never withdraws a message
once scheduled (browsers differ in whether they can), so PAUSE and STOP take effect at most
one lookahead window after the button press. See [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md).

Hardware: clock in/out and transport have been tested only against a simulated Web MIDI
device. Behaviour with real hardware, including the Squarp Hermod+ as clock master and as
clock follower over USB, still needs to be checked on the devices themselves.

## Uncertainties and provenance

- [docs/UNCERTAINTIES.md](docs/UNCERTAINTIES.md): what is unknown and what ANVIL does instead.
- [docs/RESEARCH.md](docs/RESEARCH.md): sources and the black-box observation method.
- [docs/PROVENANCE.md](docs/PROVENANCE.md): clean-room statement and repository audit.
- [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md): engine, timing and clock model.
- [docs/EXTENDED.md](docs/EXTENDED.md): Extended features and future extension points.
- [docs/USER-GUIDE.md](docs/USER-GUIDE.md): samples, processing, export and bundles, step by step.
- [docs/SAMPLE-AUDIO-ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/SAMPLE-AUDIO-ARCHITECTURE.md): ANVIL's audio system.
- [docs/SLOP-FACTORY-CORE.md](docs/SLOP-FACTORY-CORE.md): the shared audio package ANVIL depends on, and how to upgrade it.
- [docs/GOOD-BITS-DSP-INVENTORY.md](docs/GOOD-BITS-DSP-INVENTORY.md): where the Good Bits DSP inventory moved (Core).
- [docs/AUDIO-VERIFICATION.md](docs/AUDIO-VERIFICATION.md): measured audio output.
- [docs/MIDI-FOUNDATION.md](docs/MIDI-FOUNDATION.md): where the MIDI audit and roadmap moved (Core).
- [docs/DOWNBEAT-INTEGRATION-PLAN.md](docs/DOWNBEAT-INTEGRATION-PLAN.md): how DOWNBEAT adopted Core (the plan and what was done).
- [docs/ROADMAP.md](docs/ROADMAP.md): what is planned.

## Licence

ANVIL's own code and documentation are MIT licensed ([LICENSE](LICENSE)). The licence covers
nothing else; see [NOTICE.md](NOTICE.md) for its scope and the non-affiliation statement.
DSP code from The Good Bits (same author, MIT) reaches ANVIL through Slop Factory Core (MIT),
which vendors it unchanged with its own licence file.

## Development

Requires Node.js 20.19+ (22 recommended).

```bash
npm ci
npm run dev          # http://localhost:5299
npm run typecheck
npm test             # unit tests (Vitest)
npm run test:e2e     # browser tests (Playwright, Chromium)
npm run build        # static site in dist/, works from any folder
npm run build:pages  # build for https://<user>.github.io/anvil/
npm run verify       # all of the above
```

Browser tests serve two production builds (one under `/anvil/`, one at `/`) and inject a
simulated Web MIDI device. If Playwright's bundled Chromium is not installed, point
`CHROMIUM_PATH` at a Chromium binary. `e2e/audio.spec.ts` covers the Sample Bank, processing,
export and bundles; `e2e/audio-verify.spec.ts` measures real rendered audio (set
`VERIFY_OUT=file.json` to keep the measurements, `SHOT_DIR=dir` for screenshots).

## Deployment

`.github/workflows/pages.yml` runs on pushes to `main`: install from the lockfile, type
check, unit tests, browser tests, build, and only then deploy to GitHub Pages. Pull requests
run the same checks without deploying. The site is published at
<https://anvil.allmyfriendsaresynths.com/>: `public/CNAME` names the custom domain and is
copied into every build, and its presence makes the workflow build for the domain root (`/`).
Without it the build would use `/<repository>/`. The build itself uses relative asset paths
by default, so `npm run build` output also works from any folder.

One-time setup on GitHub: **Settings ▸ Pages ▸ Build and deployment ▸ Source: GitHub
Actions**, and **Custom domain: anvil.allmyfriendsaresynths.com** with **Enforce HTTPS**.
DNS: a `CNAME` record for `anvil` pointing to `clickysteve.github.io`.

# SCUMM Explorer

A Windows desktop tool (C#/.NET 8, WinForms) for browsing and visualizing resources from classic LucasArts SCUMM engine games.

## Supported games

- **Maniac Mansion (DOS)** - SCUMM v1 (the original "old bundle" release) and v2 (the enhanced re-release) - full support: rooms, walk boxes, objects, scripts, room/object images, costumes, and sound
- **Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders** - SCUMM v2 "old bundle" (EGA, Amiga, and DOS German releases) and SCUMM v3 small-header (FM-TOWNS) - full support across both container families
- **Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade: The Graphic Adventure** - SCUMM v3 (VGA, EGA, EGA Demo, and FM-TOWNS releases)
- **Loom** - SCUMM v3 (FM-TOWNS and EGA Demo releases) and SCUMM v4 (the VGA/CD "Talkie" re-release)
- **Passport to Adventure** - SCUMM v4, a 1990 LucasArts demo compilation disc
- **Monkey Island 1** - SCUMM v4 (plus the EGA Demo release)
- **Monkey Island 2: LeChuck's Revenge** - SCUMM v5 (plus the Demo release)
- **Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis** - SCUMM v5 (plus the Floppy Demo release)
- **Sam & Max Hit the Road** - SCUMM v6 (full support: rooms, boxes, palettes, object images, costumes, script decompilation, and audio playback)
- **Day of the Tentacle** - SCUMM v6 (same full support as Sam & Max)
- **Full Throttle** - SCUMM v7 (full support: rooms, boxes, palettes, object images (`OBIM`/`IMHD`), animated costumes (`AKOS`, all 3 codecs), objects (`CDHD`+`IMHD`), script decompilation, and audio playback - plus its `.SAN` cutscene videos and `.NUT` fonts/sprites, see Features below)
- **The Dig** - SCUMM v7.5 (same full support as Full Throttle - despite the "7.5" nickname, its resource format, object headers, and script opcodes are byte-for-byte identical to v7's, confirmed against real game data, so no extra code was needed)
- **The Curse of Monkey Island** - SCUMM v8 (full support: rooms, boxes, palettes, object headers, animated costumes (`AKOS`), object image rendering (`IMAG`/`WRAP`/`OFFS` chain), and script decompilation - v8 restructured the format substantially from v7 (room-local scripts moved into a separate `RMSC` resource, object images moved off the old per-state blocks, walk-boxes and room headers widened to 32-bit fields), all confirmed working against real game data)

Not every viewer is fully supported for every single game above - some of the earliest formats, and some of the demo releases in particular, have partial support (most notably Loom's EGA Demo, whose global scripts only decode about half cleanly - likely genuinely corrupt/leftover data in that early 1990 build, not a parser bug). If something doesn't decode, the tool will generally say so rather than show you garbage.

Each game uses one of four resource container formats and encryption schemes (the pre-block "old bundle" format; the small-header format; the "new directory" format; and the `LECF`-wrapped variant of "new directory" used by the last three games); the tool auto-detects the game and format from the input file (matching ScummVM's own MD5-based detection where possible, falling back to trying known keys otherwise) - just Browse to a file and it loads automatically.

## Features

- Browse the full resource tree of any room file, index file, bundled disk file, or `.SAN`/`.NUT` file
- View and export room/object images, palettes, and Z-plane occlusion masks
- View walk-box pathfinding data and the box adjacency matrix
- View and export costume sprites, frame by frame
- View and export bitmap fonts - as a full character map or a single glyph, as PNG (with transparency) or 256-color BMP
- View index-file directory tables - room/script/sound/costume/charset directories, global objects, pre-declared arrays (`AARY`), and audio resource names (`ANAM`)
- Disassemble scripts (global scripts, room entry/exit scripts, local scripts, object verb scripts) into readable pseudo-bytecode, with a split view showing the hex bytes alongside the decompiled listing - selecting a line highlights exactly which bytes it came from
- Play, stop, and save audio as a `.wav`/`.mid` file, across every format used by these games:
  - PC speaker/PCjr tones and AdLib music (`WA`/`AD`, v3/v4)
  - Per-driver MIDI sound resources (`SOU`/`ADL`/`ROL`/`SPK`/`MIDI`, v5/v6)
  - iMUSE digital audio (`SOUN` > `iMUS`, The Dig)
  - Raw digitized speech (`SOUN` > a bare Creative Voice File, Full Throttle; and standalone `MONSTER.SOU` speech files, Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis/Full Throttle)
  - Amiga sample-driver synthesis (Zak McKracken's Amiga port)
- Play `.SAN` cutscene videos (Full Throttle, The Dig, The Curse of Monkey Island) in a resizable player with seeking, subtitle overlay (where the game provides subtitles - toggleable), and export to `.mp4` (Windows Media Foundation) or the subtitles alone to `.srt`. `.SAN` files are also tree-browsable like any other resource, without opening the player: an `AHDR` node (header/palette) and a `Frames` node summarizing every chunk type across the whole clip
- View `.NUT` font and sprite packs (subtitle fonts, and Full Throttle's UI icon set) in a zoomable grid, exportable as PNG/BMP

## Requirements

- Windows
- .NET 8 SDK
- `.SAN` video export to `.mp4` needs Windows Media Foundation, present on ordinary Windows 10/11 but sometimes missing on Windows Server editions unless that feature is installed - every other feature works without it

## Building and running

```powershell
dotnet build src\ScummExplorer.App
dotnet run --project src\ScummExplorer.App
```

## Usage

1. Click **Browse...** and select a game resource file (a room file, an index file, a bundled disk file, or a `.SAN`/`.NUT` file). The game and decrypt key are detected automatically and the tree loads right away - the "Detected Game" line confirms what was found.
2. Select a block to see its decoded info. Blocks with a dedicated viewer (images, palettes, boxes, costumes, scripts, fonts, index tables) show a **View...** button; playable audio blocks show **Play**/**Stop**/**Save As...** buttons directly.
3. If detection ever picks the wrong key, change **Decrypt Value** and click **Analyze** again to override it.

## Project layout

- `src/ScummExplorer.Core` - resource parsing and decoding, no UI dependencies
  - `V3V4/`, `V5/`, `V6/`, `V7/`, `V8/` - code specific to each SCUMM engine version's resource format
  - `OldBundle/` - the pre-block "old bundle" format used by the earliest games (true SCUMM v1/v2, and v3old for Indy3 EGA)
  - `San/` - SMUSH `.SAN` cutscene video decoding (frames, audio, subtitles) and structural tree-browsing
  - `Nut/` - `.NUT` packed font/sprite decoding
  - `MonsterSou/` - standalone `MONSTER.SOU` digitized-speech file support
  - `Boxes/`, `Costumes/`, `Fonts/`, `Imaging/`, `Scripts/` - logic shared across the block-based versions
  - `GameDetector.cs` - MD5-based game identification plus decrypt-key guessing
- `src/ScummExplorer.App` - WinForms UI

# Feelers

**Put out the Feelers.**

Feelers is a browser-based interactive MIDI composition instrument. Four
lines reach out into a bank of parameter columns. Every note is assembled on
the spot from four independently moving read heads, one each on a **Time**,
**Pitch**, **Velocity** and **S/L** (staccato/legato) series. Because the
series have different lengths, directions and control elements, the
combinations keep evolving, and you steer them while they play: rewrite
material, reverse heads, loop, skip, rest, transpose, pause, mute, push lines
out of phase, and let marked values wander.

The musical model follows Emile Tobenfeld's **Dr. T's Fingers** (Atari ST,
1988) as documented in its manual: columns of 16 elements split by End of
Series and joined by Column Link, Skip / Rest / rest / Loop marks, Time as
the wait before each note, S/L in sixteenths, auto-randomisation and Restore
Last Start. Around that core it adds modern facilities (Web MIDI, external
MIDI Clock, note safety, Scale Mode, palettes, persistence) and a few
clearly labelled extensions. It belongs to a family of independent browser
instruments with *emmm*, *FrakMC* and *ANVIL*.

> Feelers is an independent browser-based interactive MIDI composition
> instrument inspired by the musical concepts explored in Dr. T's Fingers and
> MIDI-AX, developed by Emile Tobenfeld. Feelers is not an official port or
> continuation of either application and is not affiliated with or endorsed by
> Emile Tobenfeld or any historical publisher or distributor. Feelers is
> independently implemented and does not distribute the original software or
> its associated assets.

## Quick start

1. Open Feelers in Chrome, Edge, Opera or Firefox (Web MIDI). Safari runs it
   with the audio preview only.
2. Choose your output under **MIDI** (the browser will ask for permission).
   No hardware? Click **♪ PREVIEW** for the built-in synth.
3. Press **▶ START** (or Space). The default setup, *First Contact*, starts
   playing four lines on MIDI channels 1-4.
4. Watch the numbered tabs move across the series bank: each line has one tab
   on a Time, Pitch, Velocity and S/L strip. Each line panel shows the four
   values that made the note you just heard.
5. Play with it:
   - Click a pitch element and press ↑ / ↓, or type a note name and Enter.
   - Click **→** beside a head to reverse it.
   - Set **TIME×** on one line to 1.5, or nudge it to 1.010, and listen to it
     drift.
   - **PAUSE**, **MUTE**, **NEXT**, **STEP**, **RESET** and **REV** act on one
     line; **TRANS** and **VEL±** transpose it.
   - Mark elements with **SKIP**, **REST R** / **rest r**, **END**, **LOOP**,
     **?** / **¿** from the edit bar (or keys S, R, E, L, A); the **→** beside a
     column name links it to the next column of its kind.
   - Turn on **SCALE** to constrain the pitches; moved notes are marked in the
     bank and shown as `C#4 → D4 +1` in the line panels. Each line can follow
     the global scale (G), use its own (OWN) or ignore it (OFF).
   - **RESTORE** returns every value to how it was at the last Start (after
     `?` elements have wandered); press it again to undo.
   - Press **STORE** then **1** to keep the performance state; press **1** to
     return to it.
6. **☰ PROJECT** holds the demos, saving, JSON export/import, options, the
   palette, and the last nine takes as MIDI files. Hover over anything for an
   explanation in the bottom line; **?** opens the full guide.

### Keyboard

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Space | Start / Pause / Continue |
| Esc | Deselect, then Stop |
| 1-9, Shift+1-9 | Recall / store performance memory |
| ← → | Move the element selection |
| ↑ ↓ (Shift) | Change the selected value (by an octave / 10) |
| Enter | Type a value |
| S / E / R | Skip on / off, End of Series on / off, Rest → rest → none |
| A / W | Auto-randomise ? → ¿ → none, WOBBLE on / off |
| L / B / V / K | Loop or value, blank, value, Column Link of the column |
| Insert / Delete | Insert / delete an element |

## Demos

All written for Feelers (none derived from original material):

- **First Contact**: series of different lengths interlock; 3:2 bells.
- **Phase Garden**: one melody at four speeds a hair apart.
- **Clockwork**: Loop, Skip, Rest and rest, End and Column Link.
- **Drift**: auto-randomised values that wander; RESTORE brings them home.
- **Four Lanes**: gate-friendly setup for MIDI-to-CV modules, clock on.
- **Scale Lens**: chromatic material through Scale Mode, every change shown.

## Palettes

**☰ PROJECT → Palette** recolours the whole instrument: Feelers (default),
Classic (1-bit), Dark and Colour are built in; editing one makes a copy.
Palettes can be exported and imported (emmm palette files work too). A
palette is a browser preference, not part of a project.

## Hardware: Mac, browser, USB MIDI, modular

- Each line sends on its own channel (default 1-4). Set them per line.
- **CLOCK** sends MIDI Clock (24 PPQN) with Start (FA), Stop (FC), Continue
  (FB) and Song Position 0 on Stop. Pause sends Stop, Continue sends Continue.
  Clock and transport are separate kinds of message; Feelers sends both when
  CLOCK is on and neither when it is off.
- S/L is the gate length, in sixteenths of the time to the next note (8 =
  half, 15 = just before the next, 16 = touching). **NOTES** per line:
  **AS WRITTEN** keeps every length, so S/L over 16 overlaps (as Fingers did;
  needs a polyphonic voice); **MONO** is strict monophony, each gate closing
  before the next opens, which suits CV/gate interfaces; **LEGATO** overlaps
  briefly so mono voices can glide. A repeated pitch is always released
  before it is struck again.
- For a Squarp Hermod+ (or similar MIDI-to-CV module): put its tracks on
  channels 1-4, set it to follow external MIDI clock if you want its
  sequencer or LFOs in time, and try the *Four Lanes* demo.
- **PANIC** releases every note and sends All Notes Off and All Sound Off on
  all 16 channels. Stop also releases every note.
- If the interface is unplugged mid-performance, Feelers keeps playing
  silently, says so, and reattaches when it returns.

### Following an external clock (SYNC: INT / EXT)

- **INT** (default): Feelers sets the tempo and runs its own transport.
- **EXT**: Feelers follows 24 PPQN MIDI Clock from a MIDI input. Choose the
  input next to SYNC. Every incoming clock pulse (F8) advances Feelers by
  exactly one tick (24 per quarter note), so the device's clock, not a tempo
  estimate, drives every note and note-off.
  - **FA Start**: a fresh performance from the starting state (heads, loop
    counters and random seed reset), exactly like START, and remembered for
    RESTORE.
  - **FC Stop**: stops and releases every note, keeping the position, heads
    and each line's remaining wait.
  - **FB Continue**: carries on from where FC stopped. Nothing is reset.
  - **F8 while stopped** never starts Feelers; it only updates the measured
    tempo.
  - **Status**: WAITING (no clock), CLOCK (clock, waiting for Start or
    Continue), RUNNING, STOPPED (after FC), LOST (clock vanished while
    running), NO INPUT. Beside it: pulses received and the last transport
    byte. **IN** shows the measured tempo, for information only; the BPM
    control is hidden because it does nothing while following.
  - **Clock loss**: if no pulse arrives for 0.5 s while running (or the input
    is unplugged or changed), Feelers releases all notes, holds its position
    and shows LOST. It never switches to internal clock and never keeps
    playing at a guessed tempo. The next pulse carries on from the held
    position; Start or Continue from the device work as usual.
  - **CLOCK out is off in EXT** so clock is never echoed back to its source.
  - Local START / PAUSE are disabled in EXT; local **STOP** still stops and
    resets (the device's next FA or FB starts it again). PANIC works as
    always. Switching INT / EXT stops and releases everything first.
  - Song Position Pointer is ignored: Continue resumes from where Feelers
    stopped.
- **Latency.** Under INT, notes are scheduled about 0.1 s ahead with exact
  timestamps. Under EXT, future pulses cannot be known, so each pulse releases
  only the events up to the next pulse: notes leave as the pulse arrives (plus
  browser input latency, typically a few milliseconds) and their timing
  jitter follows the incoming clock and the browser. Events between two
  pulses (from TIME× or S/L) are placed using the measured pulse period.
  Fingers itself could send clock but not follow one; EXT is a modern
  facility.

**Testing with a Hermod+ (or any clock source):** connect it by USB, choose
it as the EXT input and Feelers' MIDI output, press play on the Hermod+:
the status should go CLOCK → RUNNING and IN should show its tempo. Check
that changing the Hermod+ tempo is followed, that its stop gives STOPPED with
no stuck notes, and that its continue resumes while its start restarts.

Tested only against a simulated Web MIDI device; no physical MIDI hardware
has been tested yet. Reports welcome.

## Documentation

- [docs/HISTORICAL_AUDIT.md](docs/HISTORICAL_AUDIT.md): the evidence matrix
  comparing Feelers with the Fingers sources.
- [docs/BEHAVIOUR.md](docs/BEHAVIOUR.md): the musical model, layer by layer
  (documented Fingers behaviour, choices, modern facilities, extensions).
- [docs/UNCERTAINTIES.md](docs/UNCERTAINTIES.md): what the sources leave open,
  and the choice made for each.
- [docs/PROVENANCE.md](docs/PROVENANCE.md): where every feature comes from.
- [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md): engine, scheduler, MIDI,
  Scale Mode, persistence, UI.
- [docs/DESIGN.md](docs/DESIGN.md): the design language, palettes and the
  conventions shared with the other instruments.
- [docs/FORMAT.md](docs/FORMAT.md): the project file format and migration of
  older projects.
- [docs/RESEARCH.md](docs/RESEARCH.md): the first research pass (partly
  superseded by the audit).
- [docs/MIDI-AX.md](docs/MIDI-AX.md): MIDI-AX research and a future
  Performance Mode.
- [docs/ROADMAP.md](docs/ROADMAP.md): what remains.

## Development

Requires Node 20 or newer.

```sh
npm install
npm run dev          # local dev server
npm test             # unit tests (Vitest)
npm run typecheck
npm run build        # production build in dist/
npm run test:e2e     # browser tests (Playwright; builds must exist: run npm run build first)
npm run check        # all of the above
```

The browser tests inject a simulated Web MIDI device; no hardware is needed.
If Playwright has no browser installed, run `npx playwright install chromium`
or set `FEELERS_CHROMIUM` to a Chromium executable.

## Deployment

`.github/workflows/pages.yml` type-checks, runs the unit and browser tests,
builds and deploys `dist/` to GitHub Pages on every push to `main` (pull
requests run the same checks without deploying). Pages must be set to
**Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source: GitHub Actions**.

The build uses relative asset paths (Vite `base: './'`) and contains no
hostname, so the same files work at a domain root
(`https://feelers.allmyfriendsaresynths.com/`) and under a project path
(`https://clickysteve.github.io/feelers/`).

The custom domain is set in **Settings → Pages → Custom domain**, not by a
file in the repository: for Actions-based deployments GitHub ignores any
`CNAME` file. Once a custom domain is set, GitHub serves the project site
there and points the `github.io` project URL at it; that redirect is GitHub
platform behaviour, not something the app does.

belong to their respective owners and are used only to identify them.

See [docs/PROVENANCE.md](docs/PROVENANCE.md) for what was historically
researched versus independently designed.

# Populous for Mac

A port of Bullfrog's *Populous* (Amiga, 1989) to macOS, written in Swift.

It is a **faithful port, not a remake**: the game rules were recovered by
disassembling the original program and rewritten in Swift, then checked against the
original code running in an emulator. The graphics, sounds, worlds and text are read
from your own Amiga disk image when the game starts.

**No game data is included.** You need your own Populous disk image (`.adf`).

## What works

- The whole simulation: landscape generation, walkers, settlements, fights, knights,
  the papal magnet and the computer opponent. These match the original tick for tick
  in 14 recorded scenarios.
- Divine powers: raise and lower land, earthquake, swamp, knight, volcano, flood and
  Armageddon.
- Conquest: all 495 worlds, by name, with the original scoring and progression.
- The tutorial, and custom games with the original's option dialogs: each side's
  abilities, the computer's aggression and rate, and the rules of the land.
- The original screens: title picture, "world to conquer" box, score box, the lord's
  speech, the shield with details of the person you follow, and the game's own mouse
  pointer.
- Music, sound effects and the lord's voice.
- The animated demo with its own tune, which the title falls into if you wait.
- Saving and loading games in the original file layout.

## What is missing

- In the game setup box: two players, painting the map, playing as evil, and
  computer against computer.
- Two-player games over a serial cable.
- The message icon at the lower right of the board.
- The flying creatures that cross the map.

## What is only approximate

- **Speed.** The original's tick rate has not been measured; the port runs at 8 ticks
  a second.
- **Things not checked against the original.** The simulation was compared with the
  original under emulation. Drawing, sound, scoring, the dialogs and save files were
  ported from the disassembly but not compared in the same way.

## Running it

You need a Mac with macOS 13 or later and the Swift toolchain (Xcode, or the Command
Line Tools: `xcode-select --install`).

Build the app:

```sh
./make-app.sh
open Populous.app
```

The app's Dock icon is original art drawn by `tools/make-icon.py` (needs Pillow);
`Populous.icns` is checked in, so you only run that script to change the icon.

The first time, the game asks for your disk image. To skip the question, put the
`.adf` file next to `Populous.app`. The choice is remembered.

To run without building an app bundle:

```sh
swift run Populous "path/to/Populous.adf"
```

To run the tests:

```sh
swift test
```

The tests that compare against the original are skipped unless the reference data has
been generated (see *How the port was made*).

## How to play

You are a god. Your followers (blue) share a world with the followers of a rival god
(red). You cannot command your people directly. You shape the land for them, tell
them in general what to do, and strike the enemy with disasters. You win a world when
the other side has nobody left.

### Getting started

1. On the title picture, click **Conquest**. (**Tutorial** starts a paused practice
   world with a head start and a harmless opponent; press P to begin. **Custom**
   starts a random world whose options you can change.)
2. The "world to conquer" box describes the first world, Genesis. Click
   **START GAME**.
3. The view opens on your leader. The book at the top left is the map of the whole
   world; the square in the middle is the close-up where you act.

### The basic idea

- **Flat land is everything.** Your people build on flat land, and the more flat land
  around a settlement, the bigger it grows, from tent to castle.
- **Left-click raises land, right-click lowers it.** Use this to flatten the ground
  around your people. It only works where some of your people are in view.
- **Settlements make people and mana.** A full settlement sends out a new walker, who
  looks for more flat land. Bigger settlements also give their people stronger
  weapons.
- **Mana pays for everything.** It grows with your population. The pointer on the
  rail at the top right shows how much you have and which powers you can afford.

A good opening: flatten the land around your first walkers, let them settle, and keep
widening the flat area as new walkers appear.

### Telling your people what to do

Four icons at the bottom left set what all your walkers do:

| Behaviour | What walkers do |
|---|---|
| Settle | Look for flat land and build. Use this most of the time. |
| Go to magnet | Walk to your papal magnet (the ankh). The first to arrive becomes your leader. |
| Gather | Join together into fewer, stronger walkers. |
| Fight | Seek out the enemy. |

### Divine powers

Each needs enough mana, and some worlds do not allow all of them.

| Power | Mana | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Raise or lower land | 10 | One step at the point you click. |
| Place papal magnet | 200 | Moves your ankh. Needs a leader. |
| Earthquake | 2,500 | Shakes the land under the close-up. |
| Swamp | 5,000 | Scatters swamp near the point you click. Walkers who step in are lost. |
| Knight | 7,500 | Turns your leader into a knight who hunts the enemy and burns their homes. |
| Volcano | 10,000 | Raises a mountain under the close-up. |
| Flood | 40,000 | Lowers the whole world one step. Anyone on the shore drowns. |
| Armageddon | 80,000 | Everyone marches to the middle of the world for a final battle. |

Earthquake and volcano strike wherever the close-up is looking, so move the view over
the enemy first.

### Looking around

- Click the map to move the close-up there, or use the arrow keys.
- Click **?** and then a person to follow them. The shield at the top right then shows
  their side, weapon and strength.
- The go-to icons jump to your magnet or leader, the next fight, or your next
  settlement or knight.

### Winning and moving on

When a world is decided, a score box appears. After a win the lord congratulates you
and you move on. A good score skips several worlds at once. Every world has a name,
and you can go straight to any of them: in the world box click **NEW GAME** and type
the name.

### Custom games

Two icons at the lower right of the board open the option boxes:

- **The scales**: left-click for evil's options, right-click for your own. Tick what
  that side may do, and set the computer's aggression and rate.
- **The globe**: game setup. From here you can switch between conquest and custom
  game, set the rules of the land (game options), save or load, move to the next
  map, restart the map, or surrender.

The options can be looked at in any game but only changed in a custom game.

### Keys

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| Arrow keys | Scroll the close-up |
| Esc | Back to the normal raise/lower pointer |
| P | Pause |
| M / S | Music / sound effects on and off |
| Return | Press the left button of a dialog box |
| ⌘N | New game (the world box) |
| ⌘S / ⌘O | Save / open a saved game |
| ⌘F | Full screen |
| [ and ] | Previous / next world (not in the original) |
| Tab | Switch between the original graphics and the HD graphics (not in the original; HD is an early preview) |

## How the port was made

The disk holds the game as a memory image of the running program. It was disassembled
with Ghidra, and each routine was rewritten in Swift. For the simulation, the original
routines were then run inside Ghidra's emulator, their results recorded, and the Swift
code tested against those recordings.

| Folder | Contents |
|---|---|
| `Sources/PopulousAssets` | Reads the disk image and decodes graphics, sounds, levels and text |
| `Sources/PopulousCore` | The game rules: world, people, powers, computer opponent, conquest, saves |
| `Sources/PopulousRender` | Draws the game screen, shield and dialogs; works out what the close-up shows (`CloseUp`) |
| `Sources/PopulousHD` | Puts frames on the screen with Metal, and draws the close-up in 3D for the HD graphics |
| `Sources/PopulousAudio` | The original's music and effects sequencer |
| `Sources/Populous` | The Mac app |
| `Sources/popassets` | A command-line tool to list, extract and render the disk's contents |
| `re/` | Ghidra scripts, recovered symbol names and the analysis script |

To regenerate the disassembly and the reference recordings (needs
`brew install ghidra`, and takes tens of minutes):

```sh
re/analyze.sh "path/to/Populous.adf"
```

## Legal

*Populous* is the work of Bullfrog Productions, published by Electronic Arts. This
project contains none of the original game's code or data, and is not affiliated with
or endorsed by either company. You need your own copy of the game to use it.

# Entombed

A Scala 3 port of *Entombed*, a platform game for the Atari ST written by Nick Concannon in 1991,
for the browser (Scala.js) and the desktop (JVM).

Four Egyptian tombs, in any order, then a fifth one. The tombs change while you play (they
flicker before they do), and hourglasses let you delay those changes. Seven lives for the whole
game and no saving: it was *very* hard. This port adds saving at any moment and a god mode.

## History

- **1991**: Nick Concannon releases Entombed as freeware (ST Format cover disk 30, PD libraries).
- **1995**: Olivier and Erik Bruchez disassemble and comment it, then port it to the Smaky, a
  Swiss computer also based on the 68000. The game logic is separated from the machine through 17
  external routines, the graphics are converted to 4 bits per pixel, and a save game feature is
  added (keys S and L).
- **1996**: an attempt at a PC port through a 68000-to-C translator, never finished.
- **2026**: this port.

The recovered material (original program, data, disassemblies, 1995 notes) is in
[`reference/`](reference/README.md).

## Playing

| Keys | |
|---|---|
| Arrows | walk, jump (up), climb ladders |
| Space or Ctrl | fire: start, select a tomb, shoot arrows |
| P | pause, any key to resume |
| 1 to 9, 0 | use 1 to 10 seconds of hourglass time |
| S, L | the save game of 1995 (during play) |
| Q | quit (a new game starts) |

Added in 2026 (buttons in the browser):

| Desktop | Browser | |
|---|---|---|
| F5 | F6 | save the game at any moment |
| F9 | F7 | load it |
| F8 | F8 | god mode: the man cannot die |
| F4 | F4 | unlock the fifth tomb (offered at the next tomb selection) |
| F2 | F2 | Atari ST speed (default) or 50 frames per second |
| F12 | button | switch between the Scala port and the original code (new game) |

The game runs at the speed of the Atari ST: it computed a frame in 3 vertical blanks (16.7
frames per second; the hourglass counts 16 frames per second), the title pages in 2. The sound
runs at 50 Hz, as the XBIOS played it.

## Building and running

Requirements: a JDK (17 or later), sbt.

```sh
sbt test              # unit and differential tests, on the JVM and with Node.js
sbt jvm/run           # desktop version (add --oracle to start with the original code)
sbt js/fastLinkJS     # browser version, then open js/index.html
```

## Docker

The browser version is also published as a Docker image, `obruchez/entombed` (static files
served by an unprivileged nginx on port 8080, `/healthz` for health checks):

```sh
docker run -d --name entombed -p 8080:8080 obruchez/entombed
```

The page only uses relative URLs, so a reverse proxy may serve it under a path such as
`/entombed/`. To build and publish a new version (`ThisBuild / version` in `build.sbt`):

```sh
sbt site
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t obruchez/entombed:<version> -t obruchez/entombed:latest --push .
```

## How the port was made

The port has two implementations of the game, which must behave identically:

- **The oracle** (`oracle/`): an interpreter for the subset of the 68000 instruction set used by
  the game. It assembles the commented source of 1995 (`reference/smaky/STOMBED1.L`) and runs it,
  with the 17 external routines written in Scala. A few lines are patched so that it looks and
  behaves like the Atari original (see `OracleCore.Patches`): the Smaky version rounded sprite
  positions to even pixels, displayed text at slightly different places, and kept a debugging
  shortcut to the fifth tomb.
- **The Scala port** (`core/.../game`): the same game written in Scala, routine by routine, with
  the line numbers of the 1995 source in comments. It keeps the memory layout of the original
  (data segment, BSS, screens), which makes it possible to compare it with the oracle byte for
  byte, to reproduce the original's behaviour exactly (including its reads outside tables), and to
  save a game by copying the memory, as the 1995 save routine did. Only the control flow is
  different: the original waits for the vertical blank in many loops, which a browser cannot do,
  so the port is a state machine whose states are the places where the original reads the
  joystick or the keyboard.

The differential tests (`oracle/src/test/.../DifferentialSuite.scala`) run both implementations
with the same inputs and compare, after every vertical blank, the displayed frame, the palette,
the sounds and the whole memory of the game. Long random sessions, with teleports, extra weapons
and keys to reach every kind of object, have been run on all five tombs
(`oracleJVM/Test/runMain entombed.oracle.Explore`).

Other parts:

- `core/.../audio`: the YM2149 sound chip (a Scala port of ayumi by Peter Sovietov) and an
  interpreter for the XBIOS `Dosound` sequences in which the game's sounds are written.
- `core/.../gfx`: Atari bitplanes, palettes, and the block display routine with the exact
  clipping of the original.
- `core/.../driver`: what the hosts run: save and load, god mode, Atari ST speed.
- `jvm`, `js`: the two hosts (Swing and javax.sound; canvas, Web Audio and local storage).

## Licences

See [`assets/NOTICE.md`](assets/NOTICE.md). The game itself remains the work of Nick Concannon.

# u4ed

**A savegame editor for _Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar_ that runs in your terminal, and
speaks both save formats: the original DOS `PARTY.SAV` and ScummVM's slots.**

No Windows. No Wine. No hex editor. Point it at a save, fix your party, keep playing,
and move a game between DOSBox and ScummVM in both directions.

![Character editor](docs/screenshots/character.png)

## Why u4ed?

- **Two formats, autodetected.** Give it a DOS game directory (or `PARTY.SAV`) or a ScummVM
  slot file (`~/.local/share/scummvm/saves/ultima4_enh.000`) and it figures out the rest.
  Pointing it at the ScummVM saves directory lists the slots with their names.
- **Export to the other format.** Started in ScummVM and want to finish in DOSBox, or carry
  your Avatar on to Ultima V? `Ctrl+E` writes a classic `PARTY.SAV` + `MONSTERS.SAV`.
  Coming from DOS? The same key creates a ScummVM slot, with a name and thumbnail so it
  shows up in ScummVM's load menu.
- **Every save is a version.** The same bzip2 version history as
  [u3edit](../u3edit): readable change logs, one-key restore, and your game's own saves are
  captured as well.
- **Plays nice while you play.** If ScummVM or the game saved while the editor was open, u4ed
  merges your edits on top of the new state field by field instead of throwing away your progress.
  `Ctrl+R` reloads while you play.
- **Byte-exact.** Only the fields you touch change. In ScummVM slots, the monster tables,
  metadata and thumbnail are carried over untouched. A no-op save leaves the file
  bit-for-bit identical.

## ⏳ The version history

![Version history](docs/screenshots/history.png)

- **Every save adds a version.** Each one is a small bzip2 tarball in `.u4ed-history/` next to
  the save. ScummVM slots get one folder per slot.
- **Your originals are always version 1.**
- **Game saves are captured.** If the game wrote the files since the last version, that state
  is recorded as *"Changed outside u4ed"* before anything is overwritten. Above: ScummVM
  autosaved after the party walked two steps, and u4ed kept both that save and the user's edits.
- **Readable change logs.** For example `Jaana: status Poisoned → Good, hit points 143 → 400`,
  `gold 1337 → 9999` or `+rune of Valor`.
- **Restore any version** with `F5` → `r`. The restore is itself a new version, so it can be undone too.
- **No lock-in.** `tar -xjf` gets your files back without u4ed.

## Features

| Inventory | Magic |
|---|---|
| ![Inventory](docs/screenshots/inventory.png) | ![Magic](docs/screenshots/magic.png) |
| **Virtues** | **World** |
| ![Virtues](docs/screenshots/virtues.png) | ![World](docs/screenshots/world.png) |

- **Characters (all 8):** name, sex, class, status (Good / Poisoned / Sleeping / Dead), HP,
  max HP, XP, Str, Dex, Int, MP, equipped weapon and armour, derived level
- **Inventory:** food, gold, torches, gems, keys, sextants, all armour and weapon stocks
- **Magic:** all 8 reagents and all 26 spell mixtures
- **Virtues:** karma for all eight virtues (0 = elevated, i.e. partial Avatarhood), the eight runes,
  the eight stones, and the quest items (Bell, Book, Candle, the three-part key, Silver Horn,
  Wheel, Skull)
- **World:** moves, position, party size, transport, both moon phases, ship hull
- **`F3` heal:** status Good and full HP. **`F4`:** revert one character.
- **Export dialog** with a suggested free ScummVM slot:

![Export](docs/screenshots/export.png)

## Installation

Requires Python ≥ 3.10 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

```sh
cd u4ed
uv run u4ed ~/.local/share/scummvm/saves/ultima4_enh.000   # a ScummVM slot
uv run u4ed ~/dos/ultima4                                   # a DOS game dir
```

`uv tool install .` puts `u4ed` on your PATH.

## Usage

```sh
u4ed PATH                                    # open the TUI (format autodetected)
u4ed PATH --dump                             # print party, inventory, virtues
u4ed ~/.local/share/scummvm/saves            # lists the ScummVM slots to choose from
u4ed SLOT --export ~/dos/ultima4-copy/       # ScummVM -> PARTY.SAV + MONSTERS.SAV
u4ed ~/dos/ultima4 --export ~/.local/share/scummvm/saves/ultima4_enh.007 --name "From DOS"
```

`--export` refuses to overwrite existing files unless you add `--force`.

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `↑` / `↓` | select a character (★ = in the party) |
| `Ctrl+S` / `F2` | save (adds a history version) |
| `F3` | heal the selected character |
| `F4` | revert the selected character |
| `F5` | version history |
| `Ctrl+R` / `F6` | reload from disk |
| `Ctrl+E` | export to the other format |
| `Ctrl+P` | command palette |
| `Ctrl+Q` | quit |

### Export limitations

The conversion works for saves made **on the surface** of Britannia. Inside a town or a dungeon,
the DOS game keeps extra state in `OUTMONST.SAV`/`DNGMAP.SAV` that ScummVM doesn't store, so
u4ed refuses: walk outside, save, and export that save. Editing works everywhere.

## File formats

**Original `PARTY.SAV`** (502 bytes, little-endian): `u32` unknown, `u32` moves, 8 × 39-byte
player records (hp, hpMax, xp, str, dex, int, mp, unknown, weapon, armour as `u16`; name[16];
sex `0x0B`/`0x0C`, class 0-7, status `G P S D`), food (`u32`, hundredths), gold, karma[8],
torches, gems, keys, sextants, armour[8], weapons[16], reagents[8], mixtures[26], items
(bitmask), x, y, stones, runes, members, transport, balloon, Trammel, Felucca, hull, lbIntro,
lastCamp, lastReagent, lastMeditation, lastVirtue, dngx, dngy, orientation, dnglevel, location.

**ScummVM slot** (gzip): bytes `0x000-0x1D1` are identical to `PARTY.SAV`. Then come a location
chain (`u8` count + x/y/z/map per level, world first), orientation, items, stones, runes, the
same 11 `u16` fields, then one `"MONS"` + 256-byte monster table per map (the `MONSTERS.SAV`
layout), then ScummVM's extended header (`SVMCR`, slot name, date, play time, `THMB` thumbnail).
The offset of that header is stored in the last 4 bytes.

Sources: ScummVM `engines/ultima/ultima4/filesys/savegame.{h,cpp}`, `engines/metaengine.cpp` and
`graphics/thumbnail.cpp`, plus xu4's `savegame.cpp`. Verified against real DOS and ScummVM saves
(`tests/fixtures`).

## Development

```sh
uv run pytest                          # model, formats, export round trips, headless TUI tests
uv run python scripts/make_demo.py     # rebuild the demo saves (both formats)
uv run python scripts/screenshots.py   # re-render docs/screenshots (needs inkscape)
```

The screenshots show the demo party from `tests/fixtures/demo`: the Avatar, *Werdna* (yes, that
one), adventuring with Iolo, Shamino, Dupre, Mariah, Geoffrey, Jaana and Katrina.

# roth_c — the engine and its native host

This tree builds `roth` (Linux) and `rothc.exe` (Windows), the native executable that runs
_Realms of the Haunting_ from its original game files. It has three parts:

| path            | contents                                                                                                                                          |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/engine/`   | the reconstructed game engine (see the fidelity note in the top-level README; this code does not change except as evidenced fidelity fixes)       |
| `src/data/`     | the engine's reconstructed static data as named and typed C                                                                                       |
| `src/platform/` | the native host: SDL3 video/input/audio, the DOS-era services the engine expects (files, memory, timers, interrupts), and the mod plugin platform |

The `engine` and `data` are the two parts that are considered byte-verified and faithful to the original. The `platform` part naturally is the area that had to be
modernized and it is the part allowing native support on modern systems.

## Building

The executable by default will be built as "mod-ready", just meaning it is set up with the
modding platform. If desired, you can still build the executable without the modding infrastructure.

One-time prerequisite, the 32-bit SDL3 (the engine is a 32-bit program; see the top-level
README for why):

```
../tools/build_sdl3_i386.sh     # builds third_party/sdl3-i386 (needs cmake, git, network,
                                # and 32-bit X11/ALSA/PipeWire/Mesa client libraries)
```

Then one of these:

```
make                    # the default mod-ready engine (roth)
make FLAVOR=vanilla     # the vanilla engine (roth-vanilla): no mod infrastructure at all
make dist               # the release bundle in dist/: stripped `roth`, bundled libSDL3.so.0,
                        # gm.sf2, README_ROTHC.txt, and an empty mods/ folder
make viewer             # optional: the headless-mode dev viewer (needs system SDL2)
```

The link self-checks: the moddable binary asserts it contains the mod platform's function
padding, the vanilla binary asserts it contains none, and both assert the absence of
development-harness symbols.

### The Windows build (`CROSS=mingw`)

The Windows executable is cross-compiled from Linux with the MinGW i686 toolchain
(`i686-w64-mingw32-gcc`; package `gcc-mingw-w64-i686` on Debian/Ubuntu). One-time prerequisite,
the win32 SDL3:

```
../tools/build_sdl3_win32.sh    # builds third_party/sdl3-win32 (needs cmake, git, network)
```

Then the same targets with `CROSS=mingw`:

```
make CROSS=mingw                    # the mod-ready Windows engine (rothc.exe)
make CROSS=mingw FLAVOR=vanilla     # the vanilla Windows engine (rothc-vanilla.exe)
make CROSS=mingw dist-win           # the Windows bundle in dist-win/: stripped rothc.exe,
                                    # SDL3.dll, gm.sf2, README_ROTHC.txt, and an empty mods/ folder
```

Building **on** a Windows PC: run the same cross-build inside
[WSL](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/) — it is a full Linux environment, the
instructions above apply unchanged, and the resulting `rothc.exe` runs directly on the same
machine. A native MSYS2 build has not been validated.

Windows-specific notes:

- The engine stores absolute pointers in its reconstructed data, so it requires real memory at a
  set of fixed low addresses. On Windows the executable itself is laid out to make the loader
  reserve them: it is based low with a zero-fill `.arena` section covering the fixed window (a
  generated linker script — `tools/gen_win32_arena_ld.sh` — places it) and ASLR disabled. A
  post-link gate (`tools/pe_arena_gate.sh`) re-checks that geometry on every build, and the
  engine validates it again at startup. If you change link flags or the toolchain and the gate
  fails, that is the gate doing its job.
- `rothc.exe` is a windowed program (no console). To capture its log output, run it from a
  command prompt as `rothc.exe > log.txt 2>&1`. The `--trace` switch additionally logs every
  DOS-era service call the engine makes — the first tool to reach for on file or path problems.
- The application icon and version resource embed automatically when `res/rothc.ico` exists;
  without it the build is simply icon-less.

## Running

The engine finds the game by looking for `CONFIG.INI`:

1. **Beside the executable** - the product case: the binary sits in the game's `ROTH` directory.
2. **`--game-dir DIR`** - point it anywhere.
3. **`ROTH_DEV_GAME_DIR`** - an environment variable naming a fallback install; convenient when
   running the freshly built binary from the repository.

Common switches:

| switch              | effect                                                                                                  |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| _(none)_            | windowed, mods loaded from `<game dir>/mods/`                                                           |
| `--scale N`         | initial window scale (default: auto-fit)                                                                |
| `--sf2 FILE`        | use a specific SoundFont (otherwise: `ROTH_SF2` env, `gm.sf2` beside the binary, or a system soundfont) |
| `--no-mods`         | start with the mod platform inert (`ROTH_MODS=0` does the same)                                         |
| `--list-mods`       | resolve and print the installed mods, then exit                                                         |
| `--strict-mods`     | make mod-validation warnings fatal                                                                      |
| `--dump-mod-chains` | print the resolved function-override chains at boot                                                     |
| `--headless`        | no window; publishes the framebuffer to shared memory for the dev viewer                                |

## The dev viewer (optional)

`src/platform/viewer/` contains a small SDL2 viewer (`roth-view`) that attaches to a
`--headless` engine's shared-memory framebuffer, which can be useful when working on the platform layer.

This can be built with `make viewer`. It also needs the system's 64-bit SDL2 development package.

## Modding

The mod platform's public face lives in [`../sdk/`](../sdk/) — start with
[`../sdk/MODDING_GUIDE.md`](../sdk/MODDING_GUIDE.md). In short: mods are native plugins in
`<game dir>/mods/<name>/plugin.so`, loaded and validated at boot; they can patch game data,
filter input, draw overlays, call engine functions through a versioned API, and wrap or replace
individual engine functions.

package entombed.game

import M68.*
import Vars.*

/** The man: movements, collisions and objects picked up (`reference/smaky/STOMBED1.L`, lines
  * 1512-2562).
  *
  * `joy` is the joystick byte read at the beginning of the frame (register D7 of the original).
  */
trait ManLogic:
  this: Game =>

  private def attr(block: Int): Int = ram.b(AttributesTable + block)

  /** `L00054` (1512): the man, once per frame. */
  def l00054(): Unit =
    if ram.w(StateMan) == 4 then
      // Dying: goes up, then falls out of the screen
      ram.setW(AnimManCounter, w(ram.w(AnimManCounter) + 1))
      val c = w(ram.w(MoveManCounter) + 1)
      ram.setW(MoveManCounter, c)
      if c < 4 then ram.setW(TombWord1, w(ram.w(TombWord1) - 4))
      else ram.setW(TombWord1, w(ram.w(TombWord1) + 4))
    else
      getJoystick()
      var joy = ram.b(JoystickState)
      if (joy & 4) != 0 then ram.setW(DirectionMan, 0)
      else if (joy & 8) != 0 then ram.setW(DirectionMan, 1)
      var checkFire = true
      if ram.w(TirEnCoursFlag) != 0 then
        if ram.w(AnimManCounter) != 3 then
          ram.setW(AnimManCounter, w(ram.w(AnimManCounter) + 1))
          joy = 0
          checkFire = false
        else
          // The arrow leaves the bow
          doProject(ram.w(DirectionMan), 1, ram.w(TombWord0), ram.w(TombWord1))
          prepareSound(0)
          ram.setW(TirEnCoursFlag, 0)
          ram.setW(NbFlechesTirees, w(ram.w(NbFlechesTirees) + 1))
          ram.setW(NbFleches, w(ram.w(NbFleches) - 1))
      if checkFire && ram.w(NbFlechesTirees) != 3 && ram.w(NbFleches) != 0 &&
        ram.w(NbArc) != 0 && (joy & 0xf0) != 0 && ram.w(StateMan) != 3
      then
        ram.setW(TirEnCoursFlag, 1)
        ram.setW(AnimManCounter, 0)
        joy = 0
      ram.w(StateMan) match
        case 0 => gereMouvements(joy)
        case 2 => jumpingMan(joy)
        case 1 => fallingMan(joy)
        case 3 => ladderingMan(joy)
        case _ => ()

  /** `gere_mouvements` (1597): the man on the ground. */
  private def gereMouvements(joy: Int): Unit =
    if ram.w(StateMan) == 4 then return
    if ram.w(TirEnCoursFlag) == 0 then
      getJoystick()
      if (ram.b(JoystickState) & 0xf) == 0 then ram.setW(AnimManCounter, 0)
    val raft = ram.ptr(D4988)
    var onGround = false
    if raft != 0 && onRaft(raft) then
      ram.setW(D4992, ram.w(raft + 0x16))
      onGround = true
    else
      ram.setL(D4988, 0)
      ram.setW(D4992, 0)
      val w0 = ram.w(TombWord0)
      val w1 = ram.w(TombWord1)
      if (attr(ram.b(cellAt(w(w0 + 6), w(w1 + 0x18)))) & 0x20) != 0 ||
        (attr(ram.b(cellAt(w(w0 + 0x13), w(w1 + 0x18)))) & 0x20) != 0
      then onGround = true
      else
        // No ground: is there a raft under the feet?
        var a0 = ram.l(D4810)
        while !onGround && a0 != -1 do
          if ram.l(a0 + 6) == Raft && onRaft(a0) then
            ram.setL(D4988, a0)
            ram.setW(D4992, ram.w(a0 + 0x16))
            onGround = true
          else a0 = ram.l(a0)
    if !onGround then
      ram.setW(StateMan, 1)
      fallingMan(joy)
    else if (joy & 1) != 0 then
      // Up: climb a ladder or jump
      if ram.b(cellAt(w(ram.w(TombWord0) + 0xc), w(ram.w(TombWord1) + 0xf))) == 0x1f then
        ram.setW(StateMan, 3)
        ladderingMan(joy)
      else
        ram.setW(StateMan, 2)
        ram.setW(NbToJump, 7)
        prepareSound(0xe)
        jumpingMan(joy)
    else
      var d5 = ram.w(TombWord0)
      val d6 = ram.w(TombWord1)
      if (joy & 4) != 0 then
        d5 = w(d5 - 2)
        walkStep()
      else if (joy & 8) != 0 then
        d5 = w(d5 + 2)
        walkStep()
      d5 = w(d5 + ram.w(D4992))
      moveMan(d5, d6, 1)

  private def walkStep(): Unit =
    if (ram.b(ManSynchro + 1) & 1) != 0 then
      ram.setW(AnimManCounter, w(ram.w(AnimManCounter) + 1))
      if (ram.w(ManSynchro) & 7) == 7 then prepareSound(0xc) // footsteps

  /** `L001E7` (1754): is the man standing on the raft `a0`? */
  private def onRaft(a0: Int): Boolean =
    val rx = ram.w(a0 + 0x1a)
    if w(ram.w(TombWord1) + 0x18) != ram.w(a0 + 0x1c) then false
    else
      val l = w(ram.w(TombWord0) + 6)
      if l >= rx then w(l - 0x20) < rx
      else
        val r = w(ram.w(TombWord0) + 0x13)
        r >= rx && w(r - 0x20) < rx

  /** `jumping_man` (1784). */
  private def jumpingMan(joy: Int): Unit =
    if ram.w(StateMan) == 4 then return
    ram.setL(D4988, 0)
    ram.setW(D4992, 0)
    val n = w(ram.w(NbToJump) - 1)
    if n == 0 then
      ram.setW(StateMan, 1)
      fallingMan(joy)
    else
      ram.setW(NbToJump, n)
      if (joy & 3) != 0 && ladderHere() then
        ram.setW(StateMan, 3)
        ladderingMan(joy)
      else
        var d5 = ram.w(TombWord0)
        var d6 = ram.w(TombWord1)
        var diagonal = true
        if (joy & 4) != 0 then d5 = w(d5 - 2)
        else if (joy & 8) != 0 then d5 = w(d5 + 2)
        else diagonal = false
        var finished = false
        if diagonal then
          d6 = w(d6 - 4)
          val moved = moveMan(d5, d6, 1)
          if ram.w(StateMan) == 4 || moved then finished = true
          else
            d5 = ram.w(TombWord0)
            d6 = ram.w(TombWord1)
        if !finished then
          d6 = w(d6 - 4)
          val moved = moveMan(d5, d6, 1)
          if ram.w(StateMan) != 4 && !moved then
            ram.setW(StateMan, 1)
            fallingMan(joy)

  private def ladderHere(): Boolean =
    ram.b(cellAt(w(ram.w(TombWord0) + 0xc), w(ram.w(TombWord1) + 0xf))) == 0x1f

  /** `falling_man` (1857). */
  private def fallingMan(joy: Int): Unit =
    if ram.w(StateMan) == 4 then return
    ram.setL(D4988, 0)
    ram.setW(D4992, 0)
    val d3 = if (w(ram.w(TombWord1) + 0x17 + 4) & 0xf) + 1 == 4 then 5 else 1
    if (joy & 3) != 0 && ladderHere() then
      ram.setW(StateMan, 3)
      ladderingMan(joy)
    else
      var d5 = ram.w(TombWord0)
      var d6 = ram.w(TombWord1)
      var diagonal = true
      if (joy & 4) != 0 then d5 = w(d5 - 2)
      else if (joy & 8) != 0 then d5 = w(d5 + 2)
      else diagonal = false
      var result = -1 // -1: continue, 0: landed, 1: still falling
      if diagonal then
        d6 = w(d6 + 4)
        val moved = moveMan(d5, d6, d3)
        if ram.w(StateMan) == 4 then result = 2
        else if moved then result = 1
        else
          d5 = ram.w(TombWord0)
          d6 = ram.w(TombWord1)
      if result == -1 then
        d6 = w(d6 + 4)
        val moved = moveMan(d5, d6, d3)
        result = if ram.w(StateMan) == 4 then 2 else if moved then 1 else 0
      if result == 0 then
        ram.setW(StateMan, 0)
        gereMouvements(joy)
      else if result == 1 then
        // L0020B: falling onto a raft?
        var a0 = ram.l(D4810)
        var landed = false
        while !landed && a0 != -1 do
          if ram.l(a0 + 6) == Raft && onRaft(a0) then
            ram.setL(D4988, a0)
            ram.setW(D4992, ram.w(a0 + 0x16))
            ram.setW(StateMan, 0)
            landed = true
          else a0 = ram.l(a0)
        if landed then gereMouvements(joy)

  /** `laddering_man` (1934). */
  private def ladderingMan(joy: Int): Unit =
    if ram.w(StateMan) == 4 then return
    ram.setL(D4988, 0)
    ram.setW(D4992, 0)
    var d3 = 5
    if !ladderHere() then
      ram.setW(StateMan, 1)
      fallingMan(joy)
    else
      var d5 = ram.w(TombWord0)
      var d6 = ram.w(TombWord1)
      if (joy & 1) != 0 then
        if ram.b(cellAt(w(d5 + 0xc), w(d6 + 0xb))) == 0x1f then
          d6 = w(d6 - 4)
          d3 = 1
      else if (joy & 2) != 0 then
        d6 = w(d6 + 4)
        d3 = 1
        if (w(d6 + 0x17) & 0xf) + 1 == 4 then d3 = 5
      if (joy & 4) != 0 then d5 = w(d5 - 2)
      else if (joy & 8) != 0 then d5 = w(d5 + 2)
      if (joy & 0xf) != 0 then
        ram.setW(AnimManCounter, w(ram.w(AnimManCounter) + 1))
        if (ram.b(ManSynchro + 1) & 1) != 0 then prepareSound(0xd) // footsteps on the ladder
      val moved = moveMan(d5, d6, d3)
      if ram.w(StateMan) != 4 && !moved then moveMan(ram.w(TombWord0), d6, d3)

  /** `move_man` (2016): moves the man to (d5, d6) if possible. The 6 cells touched (at x+6 and
    * x+19, y, y+15 and y+23) are recorded at D4842; doors are opened with keys; the screen scrolls
    * when needed. Returns true if the man has moved.
    */
  def moveMan(d5start: Int, d6start: Int, d3: Int): Boolean =
    var d5 = d5start
    var d6 = d6start
    var result = false
    var again = true
    while again do
      again = false
      var flags = 0
      var a2 = D4842
      for (dx, dy, k) <- MoveManProbes do
        val x = w(d5 + dx)
        val a0 = cellAt(x, w(d6 + dy))
        var d4 = ram.b(a0)
        if d4 == 0x20 && (x & 0x1f) >= 0xa then d4 = 0x18 // an open door's frame
        ram.setW(a2, d4)
        ram.setL(a2 + 2, a0)
        a2 += 6
        if k < 4 then flags |= attr(d4)
        else if ((attr(d4) >> (d3 & 7)) & 1) != 0 then flags = 0xff
      // The same cell must not be counted twice
      val p = D4842
      def copy(to: Int, from: Int): Unit =
        ram.setW(p + 6 * to, ram.w(p + 6 * from))
        ram.setL(p + 6 * to + 2, ram.l(p + 6 * from + 2))
      def addr(i: Int): Int = ram.l(p + 6 * i + 2)
      if addr(0) == addr(1) then
        copy(1, 2)
        copy(2, 4)
        ram.setW(D4878, 2)
        if addr(1) == addr(0) then
          copy(1, 2)
          ram.setW(D4878, 1)
        else if addr(1) == addr(2) then ram.setW(D4878, 1)
      else
        ram.setW(D4878, 5)
        if addr(2) == addr(0) then
          copy(2, 4)
          copy(3, 5)
          ram.setW(D4878, 3)
        else if addr(2) == addr(4) then ram.setW(D4878, 3)
      // Doors
      if (flags & 2) == 0 then
        var i = 0
        val n = ram.w(D4878)
        var done = false
        while !done && i <= n do
          if ram.w(p + 6 * i) == 0x20 then
            done = true
            if ram.w(NbCle) == 0 then flags = 0xff
            else
              prepareSound(2) // door
              ram.setW(NbCle, w(ram.w(NbCle) - 1))
              val a0 = addr(i) & 0xffffff
              ram.setB(a0, 0x21)
              if ram.b(a0 + 0x50) == 0x20 then ram.setB(a0 + 0x50, 0x21)
              else ram.setB(a0 - 0x50, 0x21)
          i += 1
      if (flags & 2) != 0 && ram.w(MoveManFlag) == 0 then
        // Blocked: stay where he is (and touch what is there)
        d5 = ram.w(TombWord0)
        d6 = ram.w(TombWord1)
        ram.setW(MoveManFlag, 1)
        again = true
      else
        if (flags & 2) == 0 then scrollAndMove(d5, d6)
        testTouchedObjects()
        result = (flags & 2) == 0 && ram.w(MoveManFlag) == 0
        ram.setW(MoveManFlag, 0)
    result

  /** (dx, dy, kind) of the 6 cells tested by move_man; kinds 4-5 test the bit d3 (ground). */
  private val MoveManProbes =
    Seq((6, 0, 0), (0x13, 0, 1), (6, 0xf, 2), (0x13, 0xf, 3), (6, 0x17, 4), (0x13, 0x17, 5))

  /** `L0022C` (2207): the man moves to (d5, d6); the screen scrolls if he leaves the central area.
    */
  private def scrollAndMove(d5: Int, d6: Int): Unit =
    val dx = w(d5 - ram.w(TombWord0))
    val dy = w(d6 - ram.w(TombWord1))
    val px = ram.w(PosInTombX)
    val py = ram.w(PosInTombY)
    if d5 < ram.w(D510) then
      if px >= 2 then ram.setW(D518, w(px + dx))
    else if d5 >= ram.w(D512) then if px < ram.w(TombWord2) then ram.setW(D518, w(px + dx))
    if d6 < ram.w(D514) then
      if py >= 2 then ram.setW(D520, w(py + dy))
    else if d6 >= ram.w(D516) then if py < ram.w(TombWord3) then ram.setW(D520, w(py + dy))
    ram.setW(TombWord0, d5)
    ram.setW(TombWord1, d6)
    val nx = ram.w(D518)
    ram.setW(D522, w(nx + 0x80))
    ram.setW(D524, w(nx + 0xa0))
    val ny = ram.w(D520)
    ram.setW(D526, w(ny + 0x48))
    ram.setW(D528, w(ny + 0x60))

  /** Entry of tomb_table3 for the cell at `a2`: a pointer into the tomb data or a record. */
  private def table3(a2: Int): Int = TombTable3 + sw(w((a2 - TombTable1) << 2))

  /** `test_touched_objects` (2284). */
  def testTouchedObjects(): Unit =
    var a0 = D4842
    var n = ram.w(D4878)
    var dead = false
    while !dead && n != 0xffff do
      val d0 = ram.w(a0)
      val a2 = ram.l(a0 + 2) & 0xffffff
      a0 += 6
      val at = attr(d0 & 0xff)
      if (at & 8) != 0 then
        // Fire, water, spikes...
        if killMan() then dead = true
      else if (at & 0x40) != 0 then touch(d0 & 0xff, a2)
      n = w(n - 1)

  private def touch(code: Int, a2: Int): Unit = code match
    case 0x2c => // Chest: opened with a key, gives its next object
      if ram.w(NbCle) != 0 then
        ram.setW(NbCle, w(ram.w(NbCle) - 1))
        val a3 = table3(a2)
        val a4 = ram.ptr(a3)
        val c = ram.b(a4)
        ram.setL(a3, a4 + 1)
        var t = D880
        var d1 = ram.w(D878)
        var found = false
        while !found do
          val v = ram.b(t)
          t += 1
          if v == c then found = true
          else
            t += 1
            d1 = w(d1 - 1)
            if d1 == 0xffff then found = true
        ram.setB(a2, ram.b(t))
    case 0x3f => // Extra life
      if ram.w(NbLifes) != 7 then
        ram.setW(NbLifes, w(ram.w(NbLifes) + 1))
        ram.setB(a2, 0x18)
        prepareSound(6)
    case 0x1b => // Key
      if ram.w(NbCle) != 4 then
        prepareSound(5)
        ram.setB(a2, 0x18)
        ram.setW(NbCle, w(ram.w(NbCle) + 1))
    case 0x28 => // Bow
      if ram.w(NbArc) != 3 then
        prepareSound(7)
        ram.setB(a2, 0x18)
        ram.setW(NbArc, w(ram.w(NbArc) + 1))
    case 0x36 => // Gold coin
      prepareSound(4)
      ram.setB(a2, 0x18)
      val v = ram.b(ram.ptr(table3(a2))) & 3
      ram.setW(PointsToAdd, v)
      addPoints(ram.l(D5032 + 4 * v))
      val index = a2 - TombTable1
      val row = index / 0x50
      val y = w(row << 4)
      ram.setW(D5094, y)
      ram.setW(D5092, w(w(index - w(y * 5)) << 5))
      ram.setW(D5096, 0x10)
    case 0x2e => // Hourglass
      prepareSound(6)
      ram.setB(a2, 0x18)
      ram.setW(NbSeconds, w(ram.w(NbSeconds) + ram.b(ram.ptr(table3(a2)))))
    case 0x2f => // Checkpoint, multiple-action point or switch
      val a3 = ram.ptr(table3(a2))
      val d0 = ram.b(a3)
      if d0 == 0xff then
        ram.setB(a2, 0x18)
        prepareSound(4)
        ram.setL(NonRetourAdr, a2)
        addPoints(ram.b(a3 + 1 + 0xd) << 12)
      else if d0 == 0xfe then
        val d1 = w(ram.w(FixationCounter) + 1)
        if (d1 & 0xff) == ram.b(a3 + 1) && ram.w(ram.ptr(D874)) == 0xffff then
          ram.setW(FixationCounter, ram.b(a3 + 1))
          ram.setL(D874, ram.l(D874) + 2)
          ram.setW(FixationSynchro, 0x8000)
      else ram.setB(B213760 + d0, ram.b(a3 + 1))
    case 0x29 => // Arrows
      if ram.w(NbFleches) != 0xc then
        prepareSound(7)
        ram.setB(a2, 0x18)
        val n = w(ram.w(NbFleches) + ram.b(ram.ptr(table3(a2))))
        ram.setW(NbFleches, if n >= 0xd then 0xc else n)
    case 0x33 | 0x34 => ram.setW(ExitFound, 1) // The exit
    case _           => ()
